questions.title: Balance drift
body: A calibrated 0.1 mg analytical balance reads 2.1426, 2.1427, and 2.1428 g with the doors closed. How should you report the mass?

blocks: Use a representative stable reading near 2.1427 g, retaining four decimal places. Acknowledge last-digit fluctuation if reporting uncertainty.

choices: 2.14270 g, with a fifth decimal added

questions.title: Adding salt and withdrawing the probe
body: Predict what happens to conductivity when a pinch of NaCl dissolves in distilled water and when the probe is removed. Explain both changes.

blocks: Mobile Na⁺ and Cl⁻ increase conductivity. Once the electrodes are out of liquid, the reading falls toward the air baseline. A residual film can delay the drop.

choices: Rises because neutral salt grains conduct in water, then remains unchanged
Rises as ions dissolve, then falls as electrodes leave the liquid
Stays constant until the probe is removed
Falls as salt neutralizes water, then rises in air

questions.title: Balance the reaction

questions.title: Limits of Beer’s law
body: At high concentrations the calibration bends below the fitted line. Near the blank, absorbance scatters as much as the signal changes. What do these observations mean for concentration estimates?

blocks: The high end departs from proportionality and should be diluted into the validated range. Near the blank, noise and baseline uncertainty dominate the signal.

choices: Dilute high samples into the linear range; noise and baseline variation can dominate at the low end
Extend the same fit indefinitely; instrumental noise affects only the highest standards
Convert absorbance to percent transmittance to guarantee a linear fit
Force the intercept to zero to remove both effects

questions.title: Two methods for one quantity

choices: Both measure precipitate mass, using dry and wet samples respectively

Both directly measure concentration without a model

questions.title: Molecular explanation of both plots
body: Explain the P–T trend for a sealed rigid vessel and the P–V trend during an isothermal compression. For each, describe molecular speed and wall collisions.

blocks: Heating raises average speed, frequency of wall impacts, and momentum transferred per impact. Isothermal compression leaves average kinetic energy unchanged but impacts the walls more often.

choices: Heating and isothermal compression both raise average kinetic energy
Heating only increases molecule count; isothermal compression raises mean kinetic energy
Heating slows molecules; isothermal compression reduces impact frequency

questions.title: A cooling curve turns around
body: A vessel cools from about 367 K. The probes are calibrated and functioning. (a) Explain the first segment, where pressure falls. (b) Explain why pressure could climb as the vessel continues to cool. (c) Why might pressure then settle near atmospheric pressure?
questions.figureAlt: In time order from right to left, pressure falls from 100 kPa to 91 kPa, rises to 100 kPa, then levels off while temperature continues to fall.

blocks: A. With V and n nearly constant, cooler molecules move more slowly and transfer less momentum to vessel walls.
B. Once the internal pressure drops below the surrounding pressure, a developing leak can admit air. Added moles can outweigh the effect of falling temperature.

C. Once the opening allows the gas to equilibrate with the room, the pressure stays close to atmospheric even as the gas keeps cooling. A leak is a plausible diagnosis, and the graph alone does not identify the exact hardware failure.

choices: Cooling lowers pressure; gas molecules are created by cooling; pressure stabilizes because the temperature stops changing
Cooling lowers pressure; a leak admits air below room pressure; exchange brings the pressure near atmospheric
Cooling raises pressure; a leak expels air at sub-atmospheric pressure; pressure then reaches zero
A sealed fixed-volume ideal gas curves this way because pressure is proportional to 1/T

questions.title: Heat sign from a temperature drop
body: A reaction in an ideally insulated cup lowers the solution temperature. What are the signs of qsolution and qrxn?

blocks: The cooling surroundings release heat to the endothermic reaction.

questions.title: Hess with a coefficient change
body: A → B has ΔH = −40.0 kJ per reaction as written. What is ΔH for 2B → 2A?

blocks: Reverse the sign and multiply by the same factor as the equation.

questions.title: Incomplete magnesium reaction
body: Only 80% of weighed Mg reacts, but all the added mass is used in the molar calculation. If it is exothermic and the reacted portion behaves normally, what is reported?

blocks: Heat is proportional to Mg reacted, and dividing by all added Mg produces a smaller magnitude.

choices: A value about 80% of the true exothermic magnitude
The true value because Mg was weighed accurately
A positive value because some magnesium remains
A value about 125% of the true exothermic magnitude

questions.title: Reference state
body: Which species has zero standard enthalpy of formation under ordinary standard reference conditions?

blocks: Elemental hydrogen in its standard molecular form has zero by definition.

questions.title: Heat leak during MgO trial
body: The MgO trial is exothermic and loses heat to the room, while the Mg trial is accurate. For ΔHtarget = ΔHMg − ΔHMgO, which bias results?

blocks: An MgO value biased toward zero subtracts a smaller negative number, lowering the target.

choices: Target stays unchanged because Mg was accurate

questions.title: Comparing signed enthalpies
body: The experimental value is −300 kJ/mol and the reference is −320 kJ/mol. What is the absolute percent error?

blocks: Use the absolute difference of 20 divided by the magnitude of the reference, 320.

questions.title: Expansion with two pressure stages
body: A gas absorbs 515 J of heat. It expands from 1.20 to 2.60 L against 1.80 atm, then from 2.60 to 4.00 L against 0.750 atm. Use 1 L·atm = 101.325 J. Find ΔE.

questions.title: Compression with heat loss
body: A gas loses 196 J of heat during compression from 5.00 L to 2.00 L against 1.25 atm. Use 1 L·atm = 101.325 J. Find w and ΔE.

blocks: ΔV = −3.00 L, so w = +380 J. Heat leaves the gas, so ΔE ≈ 380 − 196 = 184 J.

questions.title: Same end states, different path
body: Path A transfers +620 J of heat to a system while the system does 235 J of work. Path B reaches the same final state from the same initial state while 140 J of work is done on the system. What is q for path B?

blocks: Path A gives ΔE = +385 J. Path B has the same ΔE, so q = 385 − 140 = 245 J.

questions.title: Gas mole correction with a sample
body: For N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g), ΔH = −92.2 kJ as written at 350 K. Find ΔE when 0.750 mol NH₃ forms. Assume ideal gases and use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).

questions.title: Gas production at constant pressure
body: A reaction creates 2.00 mol more gas than it consumes at 298 K and has ΔE = −60.0 kJ as written. Assume ideal gases and negligible condensed-phase volumes. Use R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). What heat flows at constant pressure with only PV work?

questions.title: Identify the system energy balance
body: A rigid calorimeter warms as a reaction takes place. Assume negligible heat escape to the room and only PV work. Which statement about the reacting chemicals is correct?
choices: q and ΔE are negative, and w = 0.
q and ΔE are positive, and w = 0.
q is negative, w is positive, and ΔE = 0.
ΔE = 0 because the calorimeter is insulated.

blocks: A. q and ΔE are negative, and w = 0.
The chemicals transfer heat to the calorimeter. Rigid walls make PV work zero. Energy is conserved for the chemicals and calorimeter together.

questions.title: Hot metal with a warm cup
body: An 82.0 g metal sample at 96.0 °C goes into 105.0 g of water at 20.0 °C. The cup starts at 20.0 °C, its heat capacity is 28.0 J/K, and the final temperature is 25.4 °C. Use c(water) = 4.184 J/(g·K). Find c(metal).

blocks: The water plus cup absorb [105.0(4.184) + 28.0](5.4) J. Divide by 82.0(96.0 − 25.4) to get the specific heat.

questions.title: Calibrate a coffee cup
body: A cup initially at 21.0 °C holds 45.0 g of water at 21.0 °C. Add 55.0 g of water at 65.0 °C. The final temperature is 43.0 °C. Assume no heat leak and c(water) = 4.184 J/(g·K). Find the cup heat capacity.

blocks: The cup absorbs the difference between hot-water heat lost and cold-water heat gained: (55.0 − 45.0)(4.184)(22.0). Divide by 22.0 K.

questions.title: Bomb calorimeter with separate water capacity
body: A 1.80 g sample of a fuel (molar mass 60.0 g/mol) burns in a bomb calorimeter. The apparatus alone has C = 0.950 kJ/K and the 825 g water bath has c = 4.184 J/(g·K). The temperature rises 3.75 K. Find molar ΔE.

blocks: D. −550 kJ/mol
C(total) = 0.950 + 825(4.184)/1000 = 4.402 kJ/K. Reverse the sign of 4.402(3.75) and divide by 0.0300 mol.

questions.title: Calibrate the bomb, then burn an unknown
body: A 0.850 g standard releases 26.4 kJ per gram and raises a bomb calorimeter by 2.55 K. An unknown raises the same setup by 3.40 K. Its sample mass is 1.20 g and molar mass is 84.0 g/mol. Find molar ΔE of the unknown.

blocks: A. −2.09 × 10³ kJ/mol
C = 0.850(26.4)/2.55 = 8.80 kJ/K. The unknown gives q = −8.80(3.40) kJ. Divide by 1.20/84.0 mol.

questions.title: Neutralization with unequal mole amounts
body: Mix 35.0 mL of 0.800 M HCl with 65.0 mL of 0.600 M NaOH at the same initial temperature. The temperature rises 3.60 K. Use solution density 1.00 g/mL, c = 4.184 J/(g·K), and cup capacity 24.0 J/K. Find ΔH per mole of water formed.

blocks: B. −56.9 kJ/mol
HCl limits at 0.0280 mol. The reaction releases [100.0(4.184) + 24.0](3.60) J. Convert to kJ and divide by 0.0280.

questions.title: Predict the second neutralization temperature
body: Run A mixes 100.0 g of solution in a cup with C = 45.0 J/K and warms by 2.50 K. Run B uses the same cup and 200.0 g of solution with the same concentrations and twice the reacting moles. Use c = 4.184 J/(g·K) for both runs. Find ΔT for run B.

blocks: Heat released doubles. Divide 2[100(4.184) + 45](2.50) by [200(4.184) + 45]. The fixed cup capacity keeps the ratio from being exactly one.

questions.title: Thermal equilibrium plus gas pressure
body: In an insulated rigid 18.0 L vessel, 1.80 mol ideal gas starts at 295 K. A hot block has total heat capacity 160 J/K and starts at 510 K. Gas has molar Cᵥ = 20.8 J/(mol·K). Ignore vessel heat and block volume. Find final gas pressure using R = 0.082057 L·atm/(mol·K).

blocks: A. 3.85 atm

questions.title: Bias from ignoring apparatus heat
body: An exothermic reaction is measured in a coffee cup. The measured temperature rise is accurate, but the analyst omits the cup heat capacity when calculating molar ΔH. What bias results?
choices: Calculated ΔH is more negative than the true value.
Calculated ΔH is less negative than the true value.
Calculated ΔH is unchanged because the cup begins at the solution temperature.

blocks: C. Calculated ΔH is less negative than the true value.
The positive cup heat is missing from the surroundings’ heat balance, so the magnitude of the negative reaction heat is too small.

questions.title: Find an unknown sample mass
body: A bomb calorimeter with combined heat capacity 5.60 kJ/K warms 5.25 K during combustion. The fuel’s molar ΔE is −980 kJ/mol, and its molar mass is 74.0 g/mol. Find the burned mass.

blocks: The sample releases 29.4 kJ, corresponding to 29.4/980 = 0.0300 mol. Multiply by 74.0 g/mol.

questions.title: Ice below freezing with a partial melt
body: Place 150.0 g of ice at −12.0 °C into 350.0 g of water at 18.0 °C in an insulated cup. Ignore cup heat. Use c(ice) = 2.09 J/(g·K), c(water) = 4.184 J/(g·K), and heat of fusion = 333.5 J/g. Find the remaining ice.

blocks: Water can release 26.36 kJ cooling to 0 °C. Ice uses 3.762 kJ to warm to 0 °C. The remainder melts 67.8 g, leaving 82.2 g.

questions.title: All the ice melts
body: Mix 40.0 g of ice at 0 °C with 250.0 g of water at 33.0 °C in an insulated cup. Ignore cup heat and use c(water) = 4.184 J/(g·K) and heat of fusion = 333.5 J/g. Find the final temperature.

blocks: Cooling warm water to zero could release 34.52 kJ, more than the 13.34 kJ needed to melt the ice. Use remaining heat to warm all 290.0 g.

questions.title: Steam cools, condenses, then cools again
body: At 1 atm, how much heat is released when 18.0 g of steam at 120.0 °C becomes liquid water at 35.0 °C? Use c(steam) = 2.01 J/(g·K), c(water) = 4.184 J/(g·K), ΔH(vap) = 40.7 kJ/mol, and M(H₂O) = 18.0 g/mol.

blocks: Add 0.724 kJ for steam cooling, 40.7 kJ for condensation, and 4.90 kJ for liquid cooling.

questions.title: Slope and plateau lengths
body: A constant-power heater warms a fixed sample. Its liquid slope on a T-versus-time graph is one-third its solid slope. Its vaporization plateau lasts 2.5 times as long as its melting plateau. What follows?

blocks: D. c(liquid) = 3c(solid) and ΔH(vap) = 2.5ΔH(fus).
Slope is power divided by mc. Plateau heat is power times duration, and the same sample moles apply to both plateaus.

questions.title: Stop halfway through a phase change
body: At 1 atm, 36.0 g ice at −10.0 °C absorbs 7.50 kJ. Use c(ice) = 2.09 J/(g·K), heat of fusion = 333.5 J/g, and assume no heat loss. What is present at equilibrium?
choices: About 20.2 g liquid and 15.8 g ice at 0 °C
About 22.5 g liquid and 13.5 g ice at 0 °C
About 15.8 g liquid and 20.2 g ice at 0 °C

blocks: B. About 20.2 g liquid and 15.8 g ice at 0 °C
Warming the ice takes 0.752 kJ, leaving 6.748 kJ to melt 20.2 g. Both phases remain at the melting temperature.

questions.title: Condensation coupled to melting
body: At 1 atm, 1.80 g steam at 100.0 °C condenses and cools to 0 °C in an insulated vessel containing 30.0 g ice at 0 °C. Use heat of vaporization = 2260 J/g, heat of fusion = 333.5 J/g, and c(water) = 4.184 J/(g·K). How much original ice remains?

blocks: The steam releases 1.80[2260 + 4.184(100)] J. That melts 14.5 g of ice, so 15.5 g remains and the final temperature is 0 °C.

questions.title: Heat from a limiting reactant
body: For 2 CO(g) + O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g), ΔH = −566.0 kJ. React 14.0 g CO (28.0 g/mol) with 6.40 g O₂ (32.0 g/mol). Find the reaction heat.

blocks: 0.500 mol CO would need 0.250 mol O₂, but only 0.200 mol O₂ is available. Multiply −566.0 kJ by 0.200.

questions.title: Heat recovery and maximum product mass
body: A heater supplies 1.20 × 10³ kJ, of which 68.0% reaches CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH = +178.3 kJ. What mass of CaO can form? M(CaO) = 56.08 g/mol.

blocks: Useful heat is 816 kJ. Divide by 178.3 kJ per mole CaO and multiply by 56.08 g/mol.

questions.title: Reverse and change the basis
body: For 2 SO₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2 SO₃(g), ΔH = −197.8 kJ. What heat is needed to decompose 40.0 g SO₃ by the reverse reaction? M(SO₃) = 80.06 g/mol.

blocks: C. 49.4 kJ absorbed
The reverse consumes 2 mol SO₃ per +197.8 kJ. Multiply 40.0/80.06 mol by 197.8/2.

questions.title: Three-step Hess cycle with liquid water
body: Given C(s, graphite) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393.5 kJ; H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), ΔH = −285.8 kJ; and CH₃OH(l) + 3/2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l), ΔH = −726.5 kJ. Find ΔH for C(s, graphite) + 2 H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → CH₃OH(l).

blocks: Add graphite combustion and twice liquid-water formation, then reverse methanol combustion. Sum −393.5 + 2(−285.8) + 726.5.

questions.title: Hess with a phase correction
body: Combustion of 1 mol ethanol(l) produces CO₂(g) and H₂O(l) with ΔH = −1366.8 kJ. If all product water is instead vapor, use ΔH = +44.0 kJ/mol for H₂O(l) → H₂O(g) at the same reference temperature. What is ΔH per 2 mol ethanol burned?

blocks: Each mol ethanol makes 3 mol H₂O. Add 3(44.0) to −1366.8, then multiply by 2.

questions.title: Allotrope conversion with a new reaction basis
body: Burning 1 mol graphite yields CO₂(g) and has ΔH = −393.51 kJ. Burning 2 mol diamond yields 2 mol CO₂(g) and has ΔH = −791.88 kJ. What is ΔH for converting 3.00 mol graphite to diamond?

blocks: Per mole diamond combustion is −395.94 kJ. Add graphite combustion to the reverse of diamond combustion and multiply +2.43 kJ/mol by 3.00.

questions.title: Formation reaction for an ionic solid
body: Which equation defines the standard molar enthalpy of formation of Fe₂O₃(s) at 298 K?

blocks: D. 2 Fe(s) + 3/2 O₂(g) → Fe₂O₃(s)
The product coefficient is one, and the reactants are the elements in their reference states.

questions.title: Infer a missing formation enthalpy
body: For C₂H₄(g) + 3 O₂(g) → 2 CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l), ΔH° = −1411.0 kJ. Use ΔH°f(CO₂) = −393.5 and ΔH°f(H₂O(l)) = −285.8 kJ/mol. Find ΔH°f(C₂H₄(g)).

blocks: C. +52.4 kJ/mol
The products sum to −1358.6 kJ. Solve −1411.0 = −1358.6 − ΔH°f(C₂H₄).

questions.title: Fuel blend by mass
body: A 9.00 g blend is 40.0% CH₄ (16.04 g/mol) and 60.0% C₂H₆ (30.07 g/mol) by mass. Use ΔH°f in kJ/mol: CH₄(g) −74.8, C₂H₆(g) −84.7, CO₂(g) −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8, O₂(g) 0. Find the heat released by complete combustion.

blocks: A. 480 kJ
Molar combustion heats are −890.3 kJ/mol CH₄ and −1560.6 kJ/mol C₂H₆. Add the released magnitudes for 3.60/16.04 and 5.40/30.07 mol.

questions.title: Reference forms and physical states
body: Use these ΔH°f values in kJ/mol: O₂(g) = 0, O₃(g) = +142.7, H₂O(g) = −241.8, and H₂O(l) = −285.8. Which pair of reaction enthalpies is correct for 2 O₃(g) → 3 O₂(g) and H₂O(g) → H₂O(l), respectively?

blocks: D. −285.4 kJ and −44.0 kJ
Subtract 2(+142.7) for ozone. For condensation, subtract the vapor formation enthalpy from the liquid value.

questions.title: Bond energies with a triple bond
body: Estimate ΔH for C₂H₂(g) + 2 H₂(g) → C₂H₆(g). Bond energies in kJ/mol: C≡C 839, C–C 347, H–H 436, C–H 413. Use H–C≡C–H and CH₃–CH₃.

blocks: Cancel two C–H bonds. Break one C≡C and two H–H, form one C–C and four C–H. 839 + 2(436) − 347 − 4(413) = −288.

questions.title: Solve for a missing bond energy
body: The gas-phase reaction H₂ + Br₂ → 2 HBr has ΔH ≈ −103 kJ when modeled using average bond energies. If D(H–H) = 436 and D(Br–Br) = 193 kJ/mol, estimate D(H–Br).

blocks: D. 366 kJ/mol
Solve −103 = 436 + 193 − 2D(H–Br), giving D = 366 kJ/mol.

questions.title: Bond estimate followed by condensation
body: Estimate ΔH for CH₄(g) + 2 O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2 H₂O(l). Use bond energies (kJ/mol) C–H 413, O=O 498, C=O in CO₂ 799, O–H 463. Use ΔH(vap) of water = +44.0 kJ/mol at the comparison temperature.

blocks: Gas-phase estimate = 4(413) + 2(498) − [2(799) + 4(463)] = −802 kJ. Condense two moles of water for another −88 kJ.

questions.title: Heating efficiency and combustion enthalpy
body: A 5.00 g fuel sample (M = 46.0 g/mol) heats 720 g water from 20.0 to 57.0 °C. The water captures 78.0% of the combustion heat. Use c(water) = 4.184 J/(g·K). Find the signed molar combustion enthalpy.

blocks: B. −1.31 × 10³ kJ/mol
Water absorbs 111.46 kJ. Divide by 0.780 for combustion heat magnitude, then by 5.00/46.0 mol and apply the negative sign.

questions.title: Intersecting domain restrictions
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(16-4x^2-y^2)+\dfrac{\sqrt{y-x^2}}{x-1}\). (a) Describe the domain using simultaneous inequalities. (b) Sketch the domain, distinguishing included and excluded boundaries. (c) Which points belong to the domain: \((0,0),\ (1,2),\ (0,4),\ (-1,2)\)?

blocks: The region lies inside the ellipse and on or above the parabola, with the line \(x=1\) removed. The ellipse is excluded; the feasible part of the parabola is included.
Only \((0,0)\) and \((-1,2)\) belong to the domain.
answer.text: \(D=\{(x,y):4x^2+y^2<16,\ y\ge x^2,\ x\ne1\}\). The region lies inside the ellipse and on or above the parabola, with the line \(x=1\) removed. The ellipse is excluded; the feasible part of the parabola is included. Only \((0,0)\) and \((-1,2)\) belong to the domain.

body: (a) Describe the domain using simultaneous inequalities.
(b) Sketch the domain, distinguishing included and excluded boundaries.
(c) Which points belong to the domain: \((0,0),\ (1,2),\ (0,4),\ (-1,2)\)?

questions.title: Surface and horizontal sections
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=\sqrt{16-4x^2-y^2}\). (a) Find the domain and range. (b) Identify the graph as a familiar surface, including the restriction on \(z\). (c) Describe the level curves for \(k=0,2,4,5\), giving axis intercepts when appropriate.

blocks: The graph is the upper half of the ellipsoid \(4x^2+y^2+z^2=16\), with \(z\ge0\).
For \(k=2\): \(4x^2+y^2=12\), intercepts \((\pm\sqrt3,0),(0,\pm2\sqrt3)\).
For \(k=4\): only \((0,0)\). For \(k=5\): empty.
answer.text: Domain: \(4x^2+y^2\le16\). Range: \([0,4]\). The graph is the upper half of the ellipsoid \(4x^2+y^2+z^2=16\), with \(z\ge0\). For \(k=0\): \(4x^2+y^2=16\), intercepts \((\pm2,0),(0,\pm4)\). For \(k=2\): \(4x^2+y^2=12\), intercepts \((\pm\sqrt3,0),(0,\pm2\sqrt3)\). For \(k=4\): only \((0,0)\). For \(k=5\): empty.

body: (a) Find the domain and range.
(b) Identify the graph as a familiar surface, including the restriction on \(z\).
(c) Describe the level curves for \(k=0,2,4,5\), giving axis intercepts when appropriate.

questions.title: Three inputs and one output
questions.text: Let \(F(x,y,z)=e^{\sqrt{z-x^2-y^2}}\). (a) Find the domain and range. (b) Describe the level surface \(F=k\) for every possible \(k\). (c) Identify the level surfaces for \(k=1\) and \(k=e^2\).

blocks: Domain: \(z\ge x^2+y^2\). Range: \([1,\infty)\).

body: Let \(F(x,y,z)=e^{\sqrt{z-x^2-y^2}}\).
(a) Find the domain and range.
(b) Describe the level surface \(F=k\) for every possible \(k\).
(c) Identify the level surfaces for \(k=1\) and \(k=e^2\).

questions.title: Shifted saddle contours
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=(y-1)^2-(x+2)^2\). Sketch the level curves for \(k=-4,0,4\). Identify their center and orientations, and describe the regions where \(f\) is positive or negative.

blocks: For \(k=4\), the hyperbola opens in the \(y\)-direction, with vertices \((-2,3),(-2,-1)\).
For \(k=-4\), it opens in the \(x\)-direction, with vertices \((0,1),(-4,1)\).
Positive where \(|y-1|>|x+2|\); negative where \(|y-1|<|x+2|\).
answer.text: Center: \((-2,1)\). For \(k=4\), the hyperbola opens in the \(y\)-direction, with vertices \((-2,3),(-2,-1)\). For \(k=-4\), it opens in the \(x\)-direction, with vertices \((0,1),(-4,1)\). For \(k=0\): \(y-1=\pm(x+2)\). Positive where \(|y-1|>|x+2|\); negative where \(|y-1|<|x+2|\).

body: Sketch the level curves for \(k=-4,0,4\). Identify their center and orientations, and describe the regions where \(f\) is positive or negative.

questions.title: Reading contour spacing
questions.text: The two contour maps below show levels \(k=1,2,3,4\). One represents \(f(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+4y^2}\); the other represents \(g(x,y)=x^2+4y^2\). (a) Match each function to its contour map. (b) For each function, find the positive \(x\)-intercepts of the \(k=2\) and \(k=3\) level curves and their separation. (c) Identify each graph and explain how the contour spacing reflects its radial growth.

blocks: Map A represents \(f\), an upper elliptic cone. Its positive intercepts are \(2\) and \(3\), separated by \(1\).
Map B represents \(g\), an elliptic paraboloid. Its positive intercepts are \(\sqrt2\) and \(\sqrt3\), separated by \(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\).
Map A has constant spacing for equal height steps. Map B has decreasing spacing as the level increases, reflecting faster outward growth.
answer.text: Map A represents \(f\), an upper elliptic cone. Its positive intercepts are \(2\) and \(3\), separated by \(1\). Map B represents \(g\), an elliptic paraboloid. Its positive intercepts are \(\sqrt2\) and \(\sqrt3\), separated by \(\sqrt3-\sqrt2\). Map A has constant spacing for equal height steps. Map B has decreasing spacing as the level increases, reflecting faster outward growth.

body: The two contour maps below show levels \(k=1,2,3,4\). One represents \(f(x,y)=\sqrt{x^2+4y^2}\); the other represents \(g(x,y)=x^2+4y^2\).
(a) Match each function to its contour map.
(b) For each function, find the positive \(x\)-intercepts of the \(k=2\) and \(k=3\) level curves and their separation.
(c) Identify each graph and explain how the contour spacing reflects its radial growth.

questions.title: Temperature threshold
questions.text: Let \(T(x,y)=\dfrac{120}{1+x^2+4y^2}\). (a) Find the range. (b) Describe the isotherms \(T=60\) and \(T=24\). (c) Describe the region where the temperature is at least \(24\). (d) Is a temperature of \(0\) attained?

blocks: The temperature approaches \(0\) but never equals \(0\).
answer.text: Range: \((0,120]\). \(T=60\): \(x^2+4y^2=1\). \(T=24\): \(x^2+4y^2=4\). \(T\ge24\) where \(x^2+4y^2\le4\). The temperature approaches \(0\) but never equals \(0\).

body: (a) Find the range.
(b) Describe the isotherms \(T=60\) and \(T=24\).
(c) Describe the region where the temperature is at least \(24\).
(d) Is a temperature of \(0\) attained?

questions.title: Range after restricting the inputs
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(y-x^2)\), with the additional restriction \(y\le4\). Find the domain, its projection onto the \(x\)-axis, and the range. Find the maximum and all points where it occurs. Does a smallest value exist? Justify your answer.

blocks: Domain: \(x^2<y\le4\). Projection: \(-2<x<2\).
Range: \((-\infty,\ln4]\). The maximum is \(\ln4\), attained only at \((0,4)\).
There is no minimum: \(\ln(y-x^2)\to-\infty\) as \(y-x^2\to0^+\).
answer.text: Domain: \(x^2<y\le4\). Projection: \(-2<x<2\). Range: \((-\infty,\ln4]\). The maximum is \(\ln4\), attained only at \((0,4)\). There is no minimum: \(\ln(y-x^2)\to-\infty\) as \(y-x^2\to0^+\).

body: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(y-x^2)\), with the additional restriction \(y\le4\).
Find the domain, its projection onto the \(x\)-axis, and the range. Find the maximum and all points where it occurs. Does a smallest value exist? Justify your answer.

questions.title: A parameter changes the entire surface
questions.text: Let \(f_a(x,y)=\sqrt{a-x^2-y^2}\). Classify the domain and range for \(a<0,\ a=0,\ a>0\). When \(a>0\), classify the level sets as circles, a single point, or empty.

blocks: If \(a<0\), the domain and range are empty.
If \(a=0\), the domain is \(\{(0,0)\}\) and the range is \(\{0\}\).
If \(a>0\), the domain is \(x^2+y^2\le a\) and the range is \([0,\sqrt a]\).
For \(0\le k<\sqrt a\), the level curve is the circle \(x^2+y^2=a-k^2\). For \(k=\sqrt a\), it is \((0,0)\). All other levels are empty.
answer.text: If \(a<0\), the domain and range are empty. If \(a=0\), the domain is \(\{(0,0)\}\) and the range is \(\{0\}\). If \(a>0\), the domain is \(x^2+y^2\le a\) and the range is \([0,\sqrt a]\). For \(0\le k<\sqrt a\), the level curve is the circle \(x^2+y^2=a-k^2\). For \(k=\sqrt a\), it is \((0,0)\). All other levels are empty.

body: Let \(f_a(x,y)=\sqrt{a-x^2-y^2}\).
Classify the domain and range for \(a<0,\ a=0,\ a>0\). When \(a>0\), classify the level sets as circles, a single point, or empty.

questions.title: Product and composition
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=x^2e^{xy}+y\ln(x+y)\). Find \(f_x\) and \(f_y\), stating their domain. Then compute \(f_x(1,0),\ f_y(1,0),\ f_{xy}(1,0)\).

blocks: \(f_x=(2x+x^2y)e^{xy}+\dfrac{y}{x+y}\).

questions.title: A contour map with a restricted domain
body: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(y-x^2)\) on its natural domain. Find the domain and range. Write the level curves for \(k=-1,0,1\), including their vertices.
As \(k\) increases, which way do the curves move? At fixed \(x\), do equal increases in \(k\) produce equal vertical spacing? Find the vertical separations between these three curves.
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=\ln(y-x^2)\) on its natural domain. Find the domain and range. Write the level curves for \(k=-1,0,1\), including their vertices. As \(k\) increases, which way do the curves move? At fixed \(x\), do equal increases in \(k\) produce equal vertical spacing? Find the vertical separations between these three curves.

blocks: Upward; spacing increases. Separations: \(1-e^{-1}\) and \(e-1\).
answer.text: Domain: \(y>x^2\). Range: \(\mathbb R\). Levels: \(y=x^2+e^{-1}\), \(y=x^2+1\), \(y=x^2+e\); vertices \((0,e^{-1}),(0,1),(0,e)\). Upward; spacing increases. Separations: \(1-e^{-1}\) and \(e-1\).

questions.title: Recover a surface from its level curves
body: A function has level curve \(y=(x-1)^2+2-3k\) at height \(k\), for every real \(k\). Recover \(f(x,y)\) and identify its three-dimensional graph.
Find the level through \((4,2)\), its vertex, and the trace in the plane \(x=1\). Give the domain and range.
questions.text: A function has level curve \(y=(x-1)^2+2-3k\) at height \(k\), for every real \(k\). Recover \(f(x,y)\) and identify its three-dimensional graph. Find the level through \((4,2)\), its vertex, and the trace in the plane \(x=1\). Give the domain and range.

blocks: \(f(x,y)=\big((x-1)^2+2-y\big)/3\). A parabolic cylinder with ruling direction \(\langle0,-3,1\rangle\). Domain: \(\mathbb R^2\); range: \(\mathbb R\).
answer.text: \(f(x,y)=\big((x-1)^2+2-y\big)/3\). A parabolic cylinder with ruling direction \(\langle0,-3,1\rangle\). Domain: \(\mathbb R^2\); range: \(\mathbb R\). Through \((4,2)\): \(k=3\), \(y=(x-1)^2-7\), vertex \((1,-7)\). Trace: \(x=1\), \(z=(2-y)/3\), a line.

questions.title: Second derivatives with an unknown parameter
body: Let \(f(x,y)=e^{ay}\sin(2x)+b(x^2-y^2)\), where \(a,b\) are real constants. Find all \(a,b\) for which \(f_{xx}+f_{yy}=0\) everywhere.
For those choices, find \(f_{xy}(0,0)\) and all possible values of it. Does the condition determine \(b\)?
questions.text: Let \(f(x,y)=e^{ay}\sin(2x)+b(x^2-y^2)\), where \(a,b\) are real constants. Find all \(a,b\) for which \(f_{xx}+f_{yy}=0\) everywhere. For those choices, find \(f_{xy}(0,0)\) and all possible values of it. Does the condition determine \(b\)?

questions.title: The dependent variable matters
body: On \(x^3+y^3+xy+z=0\), consider \(P=(1,-1,1)\). First regard \(x=x(y,z)\). Find \(x_y,x_z,x_{yy}\) at \(P\), with \(z\) held fixed when differentiating in \(y\).
Now regard \(y=y(x,z)\). Find \(y_x\) at \(P\) and compare it with \(x_y\).
questions.text: On \(x^3+y^3+xy+z=0\), consider \(P=(1,-1,1)\). First regard \(x=x(y,z)\). Find \(x_y,x_z,x_{yy}\) at \(P\), with \(z\) held fixed when differentiating in \(y\). Now regard \(y=y(x,z)\). Find \(y_x\) at \(P\) and compare it with \(x_y\).

blocks: \(x_y=-2\), \(x_z=-1/2\), \(x_{yy}=-7\). \(y_x=-1/2\). The two first partial derivatives are reciprocals at this point.
answer.text: \(x_y=-2\), \(x_z=-1/2\), \(x_{yy}=-7\). \(y_x=-1/2\). The two first partial derivatives are reciprocals at this point.

questions.title: A prescribed normal determines the point
body: Find the point on \(z=x^2+2y^2\) whose tangent plane has normal vector parallel to \(\langle4,-4,-1\rangle\). Give the tangent plane.
Use that plane to estimate the height at \((2.03,-0.98)\). Find the exact error, actual value minus estimate, and determine whether this tangent plane underestimates the surface everywhere.
questions.text: Find the point on \(z=x^2+2y^2\) whose tangent plane has normal vector parallel to \(\langle4,-4,-1\rangle\). Give the tangent plane. Use that plane to estimate the height at \((2.03,-0.98)\). Find the exact error, actual value minus estimate, and determine whether this tangent plane underestimates the surface everywhere.

blocks: Point \((2,-1,6)\). Plane \(z=4x-4y-6\). Estimate \(6.04\); exact error \(0.0017\).
Yes: the error is \((x-2)^2+2(y+1)^2\ge0\), with equality only at the tangency point.
answer.text: Point \((2,-1,6)\). Plane \(z=4x-4y-6\). Estimate \(6.04\); exact error \(0.0017\). Yes: the error is \((x-2)^2+2(y+1)^2\ge0\), with equality only at the tangency point.

questions.title: Cancellation versus worst-case error
body: A rectangular box has dimensions \(x=2\), \(y=3\), \(z=4\) meters. Measurement errors satisfy \(|dx|\le0.01\), \(|dy|\le0.02\), \(|dz|\le0.01\). Estimate the largest absolute and percentage errors in volume.

For signed changes \(dx=0.01\) and \(dy=-0.02\), choose \(dz\) so the first-order volume change is zero. Is that choice within its allowed bound? Find the actual volume change for those three signed changes.
questions.text: A rectangular box has dimensions \(x=2\), \(y=3\), \(z=4\) meters. Measurement errors satisfy \(|dx|\le0.01\), \(|dy|\le0.02\), \(|dz|\le0.01\). Is that choice within its allowed bound? Find the actual volume change for those three signed changes.

blocks: Maximum estimated absolute error: \(0.34\text{ m}^3\). Percentage: \(17/12\%\approx1.4167\%\).
\(dz=1/150\text{ m}\), within the bound. Actual change: \(-217/250000\text{ m}^3=-0.000868\text{ m}^3\).
answer.text: Maximum estimated absolute error: \(0.34\text{ m}^3\). Percentage: \(17/12\%\approx1.4167\%\). \(dz=1/150\text{ m}\), within the bound. Actual change: \(-217/250000\text{ m}^3=-0.000868\text{ m}^3\).

questions.title: Two layers of the chain rule
body: Let \(F(s,t)=f(x(s,t),y(s,t))\), where \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^3\), \(x=t+\sin s\), and \(y=s+e^t\). Find \(F_s,F_t,F_{st}\) at \((s,t)=(0,0)\).
Along \(s(\tau)=\tau\), \(t(\tau)=-\tau\), find \(dF/d\tau\) at \(\tau=0\). Which point in the \(xy\)-plane must be used when evaluating the partial derivatives of \(f\)?
questions.text: Let \(F(s,t)=f(x(s,t),y(s,t))\), where \(f(x,y)=x^2+y^3\), \(x=t+\sin s\), and \(y=s+e^t\). Find \(F_s,F_t,F_{st}\) at \((s,t)=(0,0)\). Along \(s(\tau)=\tau\), \(t(\tau)=-\tau\), find \(dF/d\tau\) at \(\tau=0\). Which point in the \(xy\)-plane must be used when evaluating the partial derivatives of \(f\)?

blocks: \(F_s=3\), \(F_t=3\), \(F_{st}=8\) at \((0,0)\). Along the path, \(dF/d\tau=0\) at \(\tau=0\). The input point is \((x,y)=(0,1)\).
answer.text: \(F_s=3\), \(F_t=3\), \(F_{st}=8\) at \((0,0)\). Along the path, \(dF/d\tau=0\) at \(\tau=0\). The input point is \((x,y)=(0,1)\).

questions.title: A measured rate reveals the missing velocity
body: Temperature is \(T(x,y,t)=100-x^2-2y^2+4t\) degrees Celsius. At \(t=0\), a sensor is at \((1,2)\), has \(x\,\prime(0)=2\) m/s, and records \(dT/dt=-8\) degrees Celsius per second. Find \(y\,\prime(0)\) and the sensor speed.
At this same position and time, what instantaneous velocities of that same speed would make the measured temperature rate zero? Give all possibilities.
questions.text: Temperature is \(T(x,y,t)=100-x^2-2y^2+4t\) degrees Celsius. At \(t=0\), a sensor is at \((1,2)\), has \(x\,\prime(0)=2\) m/s, and records \(dT/dt=-8\) degrees Celsius per second. Find \(y\,\prime(0)\) and the sensor speed. At this same position and time, what instantaneous velocities of that same speed would make the measured temperature rate zero? Give all possibilities.

blocks: \(y\,\prime(0)=1\) m/s; speed \(\sqrt5\) m/s.
All zero-rate velocities: \(\langle38/17,-1/17\rangle\) and \(\langle-2,1\rangle\) m/s.
answer.text: \(y\,\prime(0)=1\) m/s; speed \(\sqrt5\) m/s. All zero-rate velocities: \(\langle38/17,-1/17\rangle\) and \(\langle-2,1\rangle\) m/s.

questions.title: Recover the gradient from path data
body: A differentiable function satisfies \(\frac{d}{dt}f(P+t\langle2,1\rangle)|_{t=0}=7\) and \(\frac{d}{dt}f(P+t\langle1,-1\rangle)|_{t=0}=-1\). Find \(\nabla f(P)\).

Find the greatest directional derivative and its unit direction. Find all unit directions in which the directional derivative equals \(1\). Explain why the two given path rates are not themselves directional derivatives for unit vectors.
questions.text: A differentiable function satisfies \(\frac{d}{dt}f(P+t\langle2,1\rangle)|_{t=0}=7\) and \(\frac{d}{dt}f(P+t\langle1,-1\rangle)|_{t=0}=-1\). Find \(\nabla f(P)\). Find the greatest directional derivative and its unit direction. Find all unit directions in which the directional derivative equals \(1\). Explain why the two given path rates are not themselves directional derivatives for unit vectors.

blocks: \(\nabla f(P)=\langle2,3\rangle\). Maximum \(\sqrt{13}\) in direction \(\langle2,3\rangle/\sqrt{13}\).
Rate \(1\) directions: \(\langle2-6\sqrt3,3+4\sqrt3\rangle/13\) and \(\langle2+6\sqrt3,3-4\sqrt3\rangle/13\). The given path speeds are \(\sqrt5\) and \(\sqrt2\), rather than \(1\).
answer.text: \(\nabla f(P)=\langle2,3\rangle\). Maximum \(\sqrt{13}\) in direction \(\langle2,3\rangle/\sqrt{13}\). Rate \(1\) directions: \(\langle2-6\sqrt3,3+4\sqrt3\rangle/13\) and \(\langle2+6\sqrt3,3-4\sqrt3\rangle/13\). The given path speeds are \(\sqrt5\) and \(\sqrt2\), rather than \(1\).

questions.title: Steepest increase while remaining tangent
body: At \(P=(1,1,1)\) on the sphere \(x^2+y^2+z^2=3\), let \(f(x,y,z)=x+2y+3z\). Find the greatest instantaneous increase per unit distance among unit directions tangent to the sphere, and its direction.
Compare with the unrestricted greatest directional derivative. Find a unit tangent direction with zero instantaneous change in \(f\).
questions.text: At \(P=(1,1,1)\) on the sphere \(x^2+y^2+z^2=3\), let \(f(x,y,z)=x+2y+3z\). Find the greatest instantaneous increase per unit distance among unit directions tangent to the sphere, and its direction. Compare with the unrestricted greatest directional derivative. Find a unit tangent direction with zero instantaneous change in \(f\).

blocks: Tangent maximum \(\sqrt2\) in direction \(\langle-1,0,1\rangle/\sqrt2\). Unrestricted maximum \(\sqrt{14}\) in direction \(\langle1,2,3\rangle/\sqrt{14}\).
Zero-rate tangent directions: \(\pm\langle1,-2,1\rangle/\sqrt6\).
answer.text: Tangent maximum \(\sqrt2\) in direction \(\langle-1,0,1\rangle/\sqrt2\). Unrestricted maximum \(\sqrt{14}\) in direction \(\langle1,2,3\rangle/\sqrt{14}\). Zero-rate tangent directions: \(\pm\langle1,-2,1\rangle/\sqrt6\).

questions.title: A shifted version of the quiz cubic
body: Find and classify every critical point of \(f(x,y)=(x-1)^3+(y+2)^3-3(x-1)(y+2)+5\). Give each critical value.
Determine whether any local extrema are absolute extrema on \(\mathbb R^2\).
questions.text: Find and classify every critical point of \(f(x,y)=(x-1)^3+(y+2)^3-3(x-1)(y+2)+5\). Give each critical value. Determine whether any local extrema are absolute extrema on \(\mathbb R^2\).

blocks: \((1,-2)\): saddle, value \(5\). \((2,-1)\): strict local minimum, value \(4\). No local maximum. No absolute maximum or minimum.
answer.text: \((1,-2)\): saddle, value \(5\). \((2,-1)\): strict local minimum, value \(4\). No local maximum. No absolute maximum or minimum.

questions.title: Nine critical points without nine long calculations
body: Find all critical points of \(f(x,y)=x^4+y^4-2x^2-4y^2\). Classify them and give their values.
Which local extrema are absolute? State whether an absolute maximum exists.
questions.text: Find all critical points of \(f(x,y)=x^4+y^4-2x^2-4y^2\). Classify them and give their values. Which local extrema are absolute? State whether an absolute maximum exists.

blocks: \((0,0)\): strict local maximum, value \(0\). \((\pm1,0)\): saddles, value \(-1\). \((0,\pm\sqrt2)\): saddles, value \(-4\).
\((\pm1,\pm\sqrt2)\), with signs independent: strict local and absolute minima, value \(-5\). No absolute maximum.
answer.text: \((0,0)\): strict local maximum, value \(0\). \((\pm1,0)\): saddles, value \(-1\). \((0,\pm\sqrt2)\): saddles, value \(-4\). \((\pm1,\pm\sqrt2)\), with signs independent: strict local and absolute minima, value \(-5\). No absolute maximum.

questions.title: An interior optimum and three boundary edges
body: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of \(f(x,y)=xy(4-x-y)\) on the triangle \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge0\), \(x+y\le4\). Give every attaining point or set.
Find all critical points in the interior and explain whether testing only the three vertices would find both absolute values.
questions.text: Find the absolute maximum and minimum of \(f(x,y)=xy(4-x-y)\) on the triangle \(x\ge0\), \(y\ge0\), \(x+y\le4\). Give every attaining point or set. Find all critical points in the interior and explain whether testing only the three vertices would find both absolute values.

blocks: Only interior critical point: \((4/3,4/3)\). Absolute maximum \(64/27\) there. Absolute minimum \(0\) on the entire boundary.
Vertices alone find the minimum value but miss the maximum.
answer.text: Only interior critical point: \((4/3,4/3)\). Absolute maximum \(64/27\) there. Absolute minimum \(0\) on the entire boundary. Vertices alone find the minimum value but miss the maximum.

questions.title: An interior minimum and a non-axial boundary maximum
body: Find the absolute extrema of \(f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2-2x\) on \(x^2+y^2\le4\). List the interior critical point and all stationary candidates on the boundary, with their values.
A student checks only the four axis intersections of the boundary. Which absolute extremum would this miss?
questions.text: Find the absolute extrema of \(f(x,y)=x^2+2y^2-2x\) on \(x^2+y^2\le4\). List the interior critical point and all stationary candidates on the boundary, with their values. A student checks only the four axis intersections of the boundary. Which absolute extremum would this miss?

blocks: Interior: \((1,0)\), value \(-1\). Boundary candidates: \((2,0)\), value \(0\); \((-2,0)\), value \(8\); \((-1,\pm\sqrt3)\), value \(9\).
Absolute minimum \(-1\) at \((1,0)\); absolute maximum \(9\) at \((-1,\pm\sqrt3)\). The axis-only boundary check misses the maximum; omitting interior points also misses the minimum.
answer.text: Interior: \((1,0)\), value \(-1\). Boundary candidates: \((2,0)\), value \(0\); \((-2,0)\), value \(8\); \((-1,\pm\sqrt3)\), value \(9\). Absolute minimum \(-1\) at \((1,0)\); absolute maximum \(9\) at \((-1,\pm\sqrt3)\). The axis-only boundary check misses the maximum; omitting interior points also misses the minimum.

questions.title: Extrema on an unbounded domain
body: Find and classify the critical points of \(f(x,y)=y e^{-x^2-y^2}\). Determine its absolute maximum and minimum on \(\mathbb R^2\), with all attaining points.
Is \((0,0)\) a critical point? Does the absence of a closed, bounded domain prevent this function from attaining absolute extrema?
questions.text: Find and classify the critical points of \(f(x,y)=y e^{-x^2-y^2}\). Determine its absolute maximum and minimum on \(\mathbb R^2\), with all attaining points. Is \((0,0)\) a critical point? Does the absence of a closed, bounded domain prevent this function from attaining absolute extrema?

blocks: \((0,1/\sqrt2)\): strict local and absolute maximum \(1/\sqrt{2e}\). \((0,-1/\sqrt2)\): strict local and absolute minimum \(-1/\sqrt{2e}\). These are the only critical points.
\((0,0)\) is not critical. No: absolute extrema are attained here.
answer.text: \((0,1/\sqrt2)\): strict local and absolute maximum \(1/\sqrt{2e}\). \((0,-1/\sqrt2)\): strict local and absolute minimum \(-1/\sqrt{2e}\). These are the only critical points. \((0,0)\) is not critical. No: absolute extrema are attained here.

questions.title: All critical points are on one line
body: Find and classify all critical points of \(f(x,y)=x^2+(y^2-1)^2\). Give the second derivative discriminant at each critical point.
Find the absolute extrema, if any. Describe the zero level set and the level set \(f=1\) near the origin: does it form a single smooth curve there?
questions.text: Find and classify all critical points of \(f(x,y)=x^2+(y^2-1)^2\). Give the second derivative discriminant at each critical point. Find the absolute extrema, if any. Describe the zero level set and the level set \(f=1\) near the origin: does it form a single smooth curve there?

blocks: \((0,0)\): saddle, value \(1\), discriminant \(-8\). \((0,\pm1)\): strict local and absolute minima, value \(0\), discriminant \(16\). No absolute maximum.
Zero level set: \((0,\pm1)\). Near the origin, \(f=1\) has crossing branches with tangent lines \(x=\pm\sqrt2\,y\); it is not a single smooth curve.
answer.text: \((0,0)\): saddle, value \(1\), discriminant \(-8\). \((0,\pm1)\): strict local and absolute minima, value \(0\), discriminant \(16\). No absolute maximum. Zero level set: \((0,\pm1)\). questions.title: Top-down design
body: Which decomposition best follows top-down design for a study-session analyzer?
choices: Create separate tasks for each line of Python syntax.
Choose every variable name before identifying the major tasks.
Read sessions; answer queries; report results. Then refine each task.
Write one large loop, then divide it into equal-length pieces.

blocks: C. Read sessions; answer queries; report results. Then refine each task.
Start with the overall goal, identify coherent major responsibilities, and refine them until implementation is clear. Equal size or shared syntax does not make a coherent task.
Source: L8 pp11-18

questions.title: Hierarchies
body: A design tree has root R with children A and B. A has children C and D; B has no children. Which statement is correct?
choices: B, C, and D are leaves; A is the parent of C and D.
Only C and D are leaves.
Every node must have exactly two children.
R has no children because it is the root.

blocks: A. B, C, and D are leaves; A is the parent of C and D.
A leaf has no children, even when it is closer to the root than other leaves. The root has no parent, not no children.
Source: L8 p13

questions.title: Design judgment
body: Which claim about top-down design agrees with the lecture?
choices: Several decompositions can be reasonable; hierarchies may miss cross-connections.
Every problem has exactly one correct design tree.
Stop only when every node corresponds to exactly one line of code.
A hierarchy captures every relationship in a system.

blocks: A. Several decompositions can be reasonable; hierarchies may miss cross-connections.
The lecture allows multiple designs and notes artificial boundaries and uncaptured relationships. Stop when implementation is obvious, not at a rigid line count.
Source: L8 pp14-18

body: What is printed? The symbol / in the choices means a new line.

body.code:
def double(x):
    print(x * 2)
y = double(3)
print(y)

blocks: B. 6 / None
The inner print displays 6. Because double reaches its end without return, its returned value is None, which is assigned to y and then printed.

body: What is printed?

blocks: return exits the entire function at the first match. The final return handles the no-match case only after the loop finishes.

def parts(a, b):
    return a // b, a % b
r, q = parts(17, 5)
print(r, q, r + q)

blocks: The function returns one tuple (3,2). Unpacking follows position, regardless of whether the caller uses conventional quotient/remainder names.
Source: L9 pp14-21

questions.title: Defaults
body: What is printed?

blocks: Provided positional arguments fill from left to right; omitted trailing arguments use their defaults. Zero is supplied explicitly, so it does not trigger a default.
Source: L9 pp85-88

body: Which header is invalid for the ordinary positional parameters taught in the slides?

blocks: A. def f(a=1, b):
A required positional parameter cannot follow one with a default. This is a syntax error in the definition, not an error postponed until calling.
Source: L9 pp85-88

questions.title: Local state
body: What is printed?

body.code:
def bump(a):
    a += 3
    return a
a = 5
b = bump(a)
print(a, b, bump(b))

blocks: Each call has its own parameter binding. Reassigning a numeric parameter does not change the caller variable. The returned value matters only where it is used.
Source: L9 pp65-78,81

questions.title: Reading global state
body: What is printed?

body.code:
rate = 2
def cost(n):
    return n * rate
rate = 3
print(cost(4))

blocks: With no local rate assignment, the function reads the global rate when called. It does not freeze rate at definition time. Passing rate as an argument would make the dependency clearer.
Source: L9 pp63-64

questions.title: Assignment and scope
body: What happens?

body.code:
score = 10
def add():
    score += 2
    return score
print(add())

blocks: C. UnboundLocalError before any output
+= is assignment. Without a parameter, local initialization, or global declaration, score is treated as local but read before receiving a value.
Source: L9 p77

body: What is printed?

body.code:
count = 1
def step():
    global count
    count += 2
    return count
a = step()
b = step()
print(a, b, count)

blocks: global allows assignment to the main-program count. The first return stores 3 in a; the later change to count does not alter a. Prefer explicit parameters and returns in new designs.
Source: L9 pp79-80

questions.title: Mutation then rebinding
body: What is printed?

    a[0] = 9
    a = [4, 5]
    a[1] = 8
    return a
x = [1, 2]
y = change(x)
print(x, y)

blocks: The first element assignment mutates the shared original list. Rebinding local a to a new list separates later changes; returning that new list gives it to y.
Source: L9 pp97-106

    b = b + [8]
x = [1]
y = [2]
extend(x, y)
print(x, y)

blocks: For lists, += extends the shared object. b + [8] builds a new list and b = rebinds only the local parameter.
Source: L9 pp90-98

    score += 2

questions.title: Study-session query engine

body.code: def analyze_sessions(names, minutes, queries):

body: Aggregate study sessions, then answer queries in their original order. Return a list of tuples (test_name, session_count, total_minutes). Repeated queries must produce repeated results. An unknown test returns a count and total of zero. Do not change any input list.

names and minutes have equal lengths, 0-1000. Names and query strings are case-sensitive; minutes are nonnegative integers. queries has 0-1000 entries. Use a dictionary to aggregate each test once, then answer queries without rescanning all sessions. Use only dictionary indexing/membership, loops, list append, tuples, and ordinary arithmetic; no get/items/values, Counter, comprehensions, or imports.

body.code:
analyze_sessions(["Math", "ENGR", "Math"], [20, 15, 30],
                 ["Math", "Chem", "Math"])
=> [("Math", 2, 50), ("Chem", 0, 0), ("Math", 2, 50)]

analyze_sessions([], [], ["ENGR"])
=> [("ENGR", 0, 0)]

analyze_sessions(["ENGR"], [0], ["ENGR"])
=> [("ENGR", 1, 0)]

body: Write a top-down plan, include a docstring, and test empty inputs and repeated values. Return results; do not print inside the function.
hints: Use each test name as a key and store [count, total] as its value. Initialize a missing name before updating it.
Build a separate output list by looping through queries. For missing names append a zero-result tuple; do not add missing queries to the session data.

blocks: Each input session contributes exactly once. A zero-minute session still counts as one session. Iterating over queries preserves order and duplicates. All modified lists belong to the newly created totals/results structures, so the inputs remain unchanged.

questions.title: First unique reading

body.code: def first_unique(values):

body: Return the tuple (index, value) for the first element whose value occurs exactly once in the entire input list. First means smallest original index, not smallest numeric value. If no unique value exists, return (-1, 0). Do not modify values.

0-1000 integer readings, including negatives and zero. Use a dictionary for frequencies and at most two full passes over values. Do not sort or use list count, dictionary get/items/values, sets, comprehensions, or imports.

body.code:
first_unique([0, 0])
=> (-1, 0)

first_unique([0])
=> (0, 0)

body: Write a top-down plan, include a docstring, and test empty inputs and repeated values. Return results; do not print inside the function.
hints: In your first pass, count every value with a dictionary. A value seen once so far may appear again later.
In a second pass, visit original indices in increasing order. Return at the first count of one; put the no-match return after the loop.

blocks: The first pass establishes global frequencies before any uniqueness decision. The second pass enforces earliest original index. The returned index distinguishes a real unique zero (0,0) from no result (-1,0).

questions.title: Sequential stock requests

body.code: def process_requests(stock, names, amounts, apply=False):

body: Process requests in order. Accept a request only if its item is known and the current available stock is at least the requested amount. An accepted request reduces stock; a rejected one changes nothing. Return (accepted_flags, ending_stock). When apply is False, simulate on a new dictionary and leave stock unchanged. When apply is True, update the supplied stock dictionary itself and return that same dictionary as ending_stock.

stock maps string names to nonnegative integers. names and amounts have equal lengths, 0-1000; amounts are strictly positive integers. Repeated items are allowed. Never create a stock entry for an unknown request. No printing, input, global, dictionary copy/get/items/values, imports, or comprehensions. Copy entries with a loop when simulating.

body.code:
stock = {"bolt": 5, "nut": 2}
process_requests(stock, ["bolt", "bolt", "nut", "pin"], [3, 3, 2, 1])
=> ([True, False, True, False], {"bolt": 2, "nut": 0})
Original stock remains {"bolt": 5, "nut": 2}.

stock = {"bolt": 5}
process_requests(stock, ["bolt", "bolt"], [3, 2], True)
=> ([True, True], {"bolt": 0})
Original stock becomes {"bolt": 0}.

body: Write a top-down plan, include a docstring, and test empty inputs and repeated values. Return results; do not print inside the function.
hints: Choose the working dictionary first: use stock itself for apply=True, or build a new dictionary with for key in stock for simulation.
Check membership before accessing an item. Append one Boolean per request. Only accepted requests subtract stock, and every later request uses the updated working balance.

blocks: Rebinding working = stock intentionally shares the dictionary. The simulation loop copies integer quantities into a distinct dictionary. Repeated requests see earlier accepted withdrawals. A rejected request does not reserve stock. Exact equality is sufficient for acceptance.
Source: L8 dictionary operations; L9 defaults, tuple returns, mutation/rebinding
