body: Find the volume of \(0\le y\le1,0\le z\le1-y^2,0\le x\le3(1-z)\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

questions.title: A roof over two parabolas
body: Find the volume above the region \(x^2\le y\le\sqrt x\), \(0\le x\le1\), with \(0\le z\le3(x+y)\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

questions.title: Symmetric base, asymmetric solid
body: A student says \(\iiint_E x\,dV=0\) because the base \([-1,1]\times[0,3]\) is symmetric in x. The solid has floor \(z=0\) and roof \(z=x+2\). (a) Set up the actual integral. (b) Evaluate it.

questions.title: Read the solid from the integral
body: Find the volume of \(E=\{0\le z\le3,0\le x\le z,0\le y\le z-x\}\). Use the order \(dy\,dz\,dx\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

questions.title: Cone capped by a plane
body: Find the volume above \(z=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\) and below \(z=3\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3\int_r^3r\,dz\,dr\,d\theta\). (b) \(9 \pi\).

questions.title: Facing paraboloids
body: The figure shows the cross-section of a solid with floor \(z=r^2\) and roof \(z=18-r^2\), rotated fully around the z-axis. (a) Find the intersection radius and give cylindrical volume bounds. (b) Find the volume.
questions.figureAlt: Facing paraboloids; shaded region with the boundaries stated in the question.

questions.title: Tilted top and a weighted integral
body: Find \(\iiint_E x\,dV\), where \(x^2+y^2\le9,0\le z\le x+4\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3\int_0^{r\cos\theta+4}r^2\cos\theta\,dz\,dr\,d\theta\). (b) \(\frac{81 \pi}{4}\).

questions.title: Drilled upper hemisphere
body: Find the volume inside \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le10\), outside \(x^2+y^2<1\), with \(z\ge0\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

questions.title: Rotate around a different axis
body: A paraboloid opens along the positive y-axis: \(y=x^2+z^2\). The plane \(y=9\) caps it. (a) Use polar coordinates in the xz-plane to give a volume integral. (b) Evaluate.

questions.title: Density is another factor
body: A solid satisfies \(x^2+y^2\le9,0\le z\le2\). Its density equals distance to the z-axis. Find its mass. (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

questions.title: Integrate over a conical floor
body: E satisfies \(x^2+y^2\le9,\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le z\le3\). Evaluate \(\iiint_Ez\,dV\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3\int_r^3zr\,dz\,dr\,d\theta\). (b) \(\frac{81 \pi}{4}\).

questions.title: A spherical cone sector
body: Use the supplied figure and exact restrictions. Find the volume inside the radius-3 sphere centered at the origin above \(z=\sqrt{3(x^2+y^2)}\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/6}\int_0^3\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\). (b) \(9 \pi \left(2 - \sqrt{3}\right)\).

questions.figureAlt: A spherical cone sector; shaded region with the boundaries stated in the question.

questions.title: Below the cone, above the plane
body: Find the volume inside the radius-3 sphere centered at the origin with \(0\le z\le\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_{\pi/4}^{\pi/2}\int_0^3\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\). (b) \(9 \sqrt{2} \pi\).

questions.title: A shell with a signed moment
body: The lower half of the spherical shell \(1\le x^2+y^2+z^2\le9\) has unit density. (a) Set up its first moment \(\iiint_Ez\,dV\) in spherical coordinates. (b) Find the signed value.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_{\pi/2}^\pi\int_1^3\rho^3\cos\phi\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\). (b) \(- 20 \pi\).

questions.title: Sphere touching the origin
body: The ball centered at \((0,0,3)\) with radius 3 touches the origin. (a) Give a spherical volume integral with the origin as the coordinate center. (b) Evaluate.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^{6\cos\phi}\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\). (b) \(36 \pi\).

questions.title: Distance from the origin
body: The radius-3 ball has density equal to squared distance from the origin. Find its mass. (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^3\rho^4\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\). (b) \(\frac{972 \pi}{5}\).

questions.title: Recover a Cartesian coordinate
body: A point has spherical coordinates \((\rho,\theta,\phi)=(6,7\pi/6,2\pi/3)\). Find its x-coordinate. (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

questions.title: Correct a spherical integrand
body: A student uses \(\rho^2\sin\phi\) as the complete integrand for \(\iiint_E(x^2+y^2)\,dV\) on a radius-3 upper hemisphere. Find the correct integral value. (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^3\rho^4\sin^3\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\). (b) \(\frac{324 \pi}{5}\).

questions.title: Linear combinations define the sides
body: Use the supplied figure and exact restrictions. R satisfies \(0\le x+y\le3,0\le x-y\le1\). Evaluate \(\iint_R(x+y)^2\,dA\) using \(u=x+y,v=x-y\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.
questions.figureAlt: Linear combinations define the sides; shaded region with the boundaries stated in the question.

questions.title: Elliptical radial integral
body: Evaluate \(\iint_D e^{x^2/9+y^2/4}\,dA\), where \(x^2/9+y^2/4\le1\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^1 6re^{r^2}\,dr\,d\theta\). (b) \(6 \pi \left(-1 + e\right)\).

questions.title: A nonlinear transformation
body: The rectangle \(1\le u\le3,0\le v\le1\) maps to R by \(x=u,y=uv\). (a) Transform \(\iint_R(y/x)\,dA\), including the area factor. (b) Evaluate.

questions.title: An inverse determinant is not the area factor
body: The map \(u=3x+y,v=x-y\) sends R to \([0,2]\times[0,3]\). A student multiplies 6 by \(|\partial(u,v)/\partial(x,y)|\). (a) Give the correct area integral. (b) Find the area of R.

questions.title: Orientation versus positive area
body: Let \(x=u+3v,y=2u-v\), with \(0\le u,v\le1\). A student integrates the signed coefficient in \(dx\wedge dy\) to compute ordinary area. Find the correct area. (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

questions.title: A three-dimensional scaling
body: Find the volume of \(x^2/9+y^2/4+z^2/9\le1\) by mapping it to a unit ball. (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

blocks: (a) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\int_0^118\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\). (b) \(24 \pi\).

questions.title: Choose variables from an exponential
body: Evaluate \(\iint_R(x+y)e^{x^2-y^2}\,dA\), where \(0\le x+y\le3,0\le x-y\le1\). (a) Give a suitable iterated integral or transformed expression. (b) Evaluate it.

questions.title: Six orders for one curved solid
body: E is defined by \(x^2\le y\le4,0\le z\le4-y\). (a) Write its volume integral in all six orders. (b) Find its volume.

blocks: \(\int_0^4\int_{-\sqrt y}^{\sqrt y}\int_0^{4-y}1\,dz\,dx\,dy\); \(\int_0^4\int_0^{4-y}\int_{-\sqrt y}^{\sqrt y}1\,dx\,dz\,dy\);

questions.concept: Six orders for one curved solid

questions.title: Coordinate surfaces and quadrants
body: (a) Convert \((-2,-2,3)\) to cylindrical coordinates with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\). (b) Identify the surface \(r=2\). (c) Identify \(\theta=5\pi/4\), including its restriction.

blocks: (a) \((2\sqrt2,5\pi/4,3)\). (b) Cylinder \(x^2+y^2=4\). (c) Vertical half-plane \(y=x,x\le0\), with z unrestricted.

questions.title: Choose coordinates, then calculate
body: The solid satisfies \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le4,z\ge0\). (a) Choose cylindrical or spherical coordinates to evaluate \(\iiint_E\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\,dV\) with constant coordinate bounds. Give the integral. (b) Evaluate. (c) Give its cylindrical setup for comparison.

blocks: (a) Spherical: \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^2\rho^3\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\). (b) \(16\pi/2\). (c) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^2\int_0^{\sqrt{4-r^2}}r\sqrt{r^2+z^2}\,dz\,dr\,d\theta\).

questions.title: Forward and inverse Jacobians
body: (a) At a point with polar radius \(r=2\), find \(\partial(x,y)/\partial(r,\theta)\) and \(\partial(r,\theta)/\partial(x,y)\). (b) For cylindrical coordinates, find the absolute 3D Jacobian there. (c) For spherical coordinates at \(\rho=2,\phi=\pi/6\), find the absolute 3D Jacobian.

questions.title: Six orders for one curved solid
body: E is defined by \(x^2\le y\le9,0\le z\le9-y\). (a) Write its volume integral in all six orders. (b) Find its volume.

blocks: \(\int_0^9\int_{-\sqrt y}^{\sqrt y}\int_0^{9-y}1\,dz\,dx\,dy\); \(\int_0^9\int_0^{9-y}\int_{-\sqrt y}^{\sqrt y}1\,dx\,dz\,dy\);

questions.concept: Six orders for one curved solid

questions.title: Coordinate surfaces and quadrants
body: (a) Convert \((-3,-3,3)\) to cylindrical coordinates with \(0\le\theta<2\pi\). (b) Identify the surface \(r=3\). (c) Identify \(\theta=5\pi/4\), including its restriction.

blocks: (a) \((3\sqrt2,5\pi/4,3)\). (b) Cylinder \(x^2+y^2=9\). (c) Vertical half-plane \(y=x,x\le0\), with z unrestricted.

questions.title: Choose coordinates, then calculate
body: The solid satisfies \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le9,z\ge0\). (a) Choose cylindrical or spherical coordinates to evaluate \(\iiint_E\sqrt{x^2+y^2+z^2}\,dV\) with constant coordinate bounds. Give the integral. (b) Evaluate. (c) Give its cylindrical setup for comparison.

blocks: (a) Spherical: \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/2}\int_0^3\rho^3\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\). (b) \(81\pi/2\). (c) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^3\int_0^{\sqrt{9-r^2}}r\sqrt{r^2+z^2}\,dz\,dr\,d\theta\).

questions.title: Forward and inverse Jacobians
body: (a) At a point with polar radius \(r=3\), find \(\partial(x,y)/\partial(r,\theta)\) and \(\partial(r,\theta)/\partial(x,y)\). (b) For cylindrical coordinates, find the absolute 3D Jacobian there. (c) For spherical coordinates at \(\rho=3,\phi=\pi/6\), find the absolute 3D Jacobian.

questions.title: A Gaussian over the whole plane
body: (a) Use polar coordinates to express \(\iint_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-2x^2-2y^2}\,dA\) as a limit of integrals over disks. (b) Evaluate the limit. (c) What fraction of the total lies outside \(x^2+y^2=1\)?
questions.concept: A Gaussian over the whole plane

questions.title: Recover a Gaussian parameter
body: For \(c>0\), \(\iint_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-c(x^2+y^2)}\,dA=\pi/3\). (a) Give its polar setup in terms of c. (b) Find c. (c) Evaluate the same integral restricted to \(x^2+y^2\ge1\).

questions.title: A plane makes the radial lower bound move
body: E is inside \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le4z\) and above \(z=2\). (a) Give spherical bounds, including the intersection angle. (b) Set up and evaluate its volume.

blocks: (a) \(0\le\theta\le2\pi,0\le\phi\le\pi/4,2\sec\phi\le\rho\le4\cos\phi\). (b) \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^{\pi/4}\int_{2\sec\phi}^{4\cos\phi}\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta=16\pi/3\).

questions.concept: A plane makes the radial lower bound move

questions.title: Find the missing angular endpoint
body: A spherical setup for the volume inside \(x^2+y^2+z^2\le6z\) and above \(z=3\) is \(\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\alpha\int_{3\sec\phi}^{6\cos\phi}\rho^2\sin\phi\,d\rho\,d\phi\,d\theta\). (a) Find \(\alpha\). (b) Evaluate. (c) Identify the solid using its sphere center and radius.

blocks: (a) \(\alpha=\pi/4\). (b) \(18\pi\). (c) Upper hemisphere of the radius-3 sphere centered at \((0,0,3)\).

questions.title: Spherical surfaces and their intersection
body: (a) Give Cartesian equations and any sign restriction for \(\rho=4\) and \(\phi=2\pi/3\). (b) Their intersection is a horizontal circle. Find its height and radius.

questions.title: Do not include the other cone
body: A student replaces \(\phi=\pi/6\) by \(z^2=3(x^2+y^2)\). (a) Supply the missing restriction. (b) Find the radius and height of the intersection with \(\rho=6\). (c) Give the spherical angle of the unwanted lower cone.

blocks: (a) \(z\ge0\). (b) Radius \(3\), height \(3\sqrt3\). (c) \(\phi=5\pi/6\).

questions.concept: Do not include the other cone

questions.title: Polar coordinates with quadrant information
body: (a) Convert \((-\sqrt3,1)\) to polar coordinates with \(r\ge0,0\le\theta<2\pi\). (b) Convert the polar point \((4,5\pi/3)\) to Cartesian coordinates. (c) Give a Cartesian equation for \(r=4\cos\theta\).

questions.title: Read a shifted circle from a polar boundary
body: (a) Convert \(x^2+(y-3)^2=9\) to polar form. (b) Give bounds covering its interior exactly once with \(r\ge0\). (c) Convert the boundary point with \(\theta=5\pi/6\) to Cartesian coordinates.

blocks: (a) \(r=6\sin\theta\). (b) \(0\le\theta\le\pi,0\le r\le6\sin\theta\). (c) \((-3\sqrt3/2,3/2)\).

questions.concept: Read a shifted circle from a polar boundary

questions.title: Threshold wavelength from binding energy
body: A metal has work function 4.20 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Which pair correctly gives its threshold wavelength and whether 500 nm light can eject electrons?

blocks: B. 473 nm; no
Why: λ₀ = hc/φ = 473 nm; 500 nm photons have less energy than the work function.

questions.title: Maximum photoelectron energy
body: A metal has work function 3.10 × 10⁻¹⁹ J and is illuminated at 400.0 nm. What is the maximum electron kinetic energy?

blocks: Why: The photon supplies 4.97 × 10⁻¹⁹ J; subtract the work function.

questions.title: Brightness versus photon energy
body: A surface ejects electrons under 450 nm light but not under 650 nm light. In the ordinary single-photon model, select every statement that must be true.
choices: At fixed 450 nm wavelength, higher intensity supplies more photons per second to the same area.
The work function is greater than a 650 nm photon’s energy and no greater than a 450 nm photon’s energy.
670 nm photons must eject electrons if the beam is bright enough.
Doubling 450 nm intensity increases maximum electron kinetic energy.

blocks: A, B, C. At fixed 450 nm wavelength, higher intensity supplies more photons per second to the same area. | The work function is greater than a 650 nm photon’s energy and no greater than a 450 nm photon’s energy. | 400 nm photons can eject electrons.
Why: Threshold depends on energy per photon; intensity changes photon arrival rate, not hc/λ.

questions.title: Shortest emitted wavelength
body: Which listed H transition emits the shortest-wavelength photon?

blocks: Why: Emission is downward; the largest energy drop gives the shortest wavelength.

questions.title: Read an energy-level diagram
body: The diagram labels four transitions. Select every true statement.
choices: B and C emit photons of equal energy.
For B, the atom’s ΔE is negative while photon energy is positive.
B emits a shorter wavelength than C.

blocks: C, D, E. For B, the atom’s ΔE is negative while photon energy is positive. | A is absorption. | B emits a shorter wavelength than C.
Why: A rises from 1 to 3; B is 3 → 1, C is 3 → 2, and D rises 2 → 4. Compare energy gaps, not arrow lengths on an arbitrary drawing.

questions.figureAlt: Hydrogen levels n=1 to 4. A:1→3, B:3→1, C:3→2, D:2→4.

questions.title: Find the emitted wavelength
body: An H electron falls from n = 4 to n = 2. Which pair gives the emitted wavelength and sign of ΔEatom?

blocks: D. 486 nm; negative

questions.title: Choose the invalid quantum-number tuple
body: Which tuple (n, ℓ, mℓ, mₛ) is NOT allowed?

blocks: Why: For n = 3, ℓ can only be 0, 1, or 2.

questions.title: Several tuples can be invalid
body: Select every INVALID tuple (n, ℓ, mℓ, mₛ).

blocks: Why: mℓ must lie from −ℓ to +ℓ, spin is ±½, and ℓ must be less than n.

questions.title: Invalid versus merely unoccupied
body: For a ground-state Ne atom, which description is correct? Ne has configuration 1s²2s²2p⁶.
choices: (3,2,0,+½) is allowed but unoccupied; (2,2,0,+½) is forbidden.
Both tuples are forbidden because Ne has no n=3 electrons.
Both tuples are occupied because d can hold 10 electrons.
(3,2,0,+½) is forbidden; (2,2,0,+½) is allowed but unoccupied.

blocks: A. (3,2,0,+½) is allowed but unoccupied; (2,2,0,+½) is forbidden.
Why: Quantum-number validity is independent of the electron population in the chosen atom.

questions.title: Count actual electrons with a specified mℓ
body: A ground-state Kr atom has [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s²4p⁶. How many of its electrons have mℓ = +1?

blocks: Why: Filled 2p, 3p, 3d, and 4p each contain two electrons with mℓ = +1.

questions.title: Leave some quantum numbers unspecified
body: What is the maximum number of electrons in one atom with n = 4 and mℓ = 0?

blocks: Why: There is one mℓ = 0 orbital in each of 4s, 4p, 4d, and 4f; each holds two electrons.

questions.title: Capacity and population are different
body: Select every correct statement about allowed electron capacities and ground-state Ar, 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶.
choices: The n = 3 shell can hold at most 18 electrons.
The specified set n=3, ℓ=1, mℓ=0, mₛ=+½ can describe at most 2 electrons in one atom.
Every ground-state Ar electron with n=3 has ℓ=1.
Exactly 4 electrons in ground-state Ar have mℓ = +1.
The 3d subshell is allowed but empty in ground-state Ar.

blocks: A, D, E. The n = 3 shell can hold at most 18 electrons. | Exactly 4 electrons in ground-state Ar have mℓ = +1. | The 3d subshell is allowed but empty in ground-state Ar.
Why: A full shell has capacity 2n²; actual Ar occupies 3s and 3p but not 3d. Four specified quantum numbers identify at most one electron.

questions.title: Rank an isoelectronic series
body: Which order is increasing ionic radius? Z: O=8, F=9, Na=11, Mg=12.

blocks: C. Mg²⁺ < Na⁺ < F⁻ < O²⁻
Why: All contain 10 electrons; greater nuclear charge gives a smaller ion.

questions.title: Combine ion and atom radius comparisons
body: Select every correct radius comparison using the standard main-group/isolated-ion trends.
choices: Mg²⁺ is larger than Ca²⁺ because it has fewer electrons.
S²⁻ is smaller than Cl⁻ in their isoelectronic series.

blocks: A, B, E. Cl⁻ is larger than Cl. | Fe³⁺ is smaller than Fe²⁺. | K is larger than Ca.
Why: Cation charge, anion expansion, period trends, and isoelectronic nuclear attraction must be applied to the appropriate pairs.

questions.title: Size is not set by charge alone
body: Which comparison and reason are both correct?
choices: O²⁻ < F⁻ because O²⁻ has the more negative charge.
Ca²⁺ > K⁺ because Ca has the higher atomic number.
Rb⁺ > K⁺ because Rb⁺ has its outer occupied electrons in a larger principal shell.
Rb⁺ < K⁺ because all ions with more protons must be smaller.

blocks: C. Rb⁺ > K⁺ because Rb⁺ has its outer occupied electrons in a larger principal shell.
Why: Rb⁺ and K⁺ are not isoelectronic with each other; compare their occupied shells first.

questions.title: Infer an element from an ionization jump
body: A period-3 element has IE₁=578, IE₂=1817, IE₃=2745, IE₄=11,577 kJ/mol. Which element and usual simple-ion charge fit?

blocks: C. Al; +3
Why: The large jump after three removals indicates three valence electrons; period 3 gives Al.

questions.title: Locate the core-electron jump
body: For a ground-state phosphorus atom, [Ne]3s²3p³, the largest initial valence-to-core jump occurs between which successive ionization energies?

blocks: C. IE₅ and IE₆
Why: Five valence electrons are removed before the first n=2 core electron.

questions.title: Exceptions to a simple left-to-right arrow
body: Select every correct first-ionization-energy comparison or explanation.
choices: IE₁(Be) > IE₁(B): B loses a higher-energy 2p electron.
IE₁ is normally negative because removing electrons releases energy.
IE₁(N) > IE₁(O): pairing in O’s 2p orbitals makes removal easier.
IE₁(Mg) < IE₁(Al) because the trend has no exceptions.
Successive ionization energies generally increase for a given element.

blocks: A, C, E. IE₁(Be) > IE₁(B): B loses a higher-energy 2p electron. | IE₁(N) > IE₁(O): pairing in O’s 2p orbitals makes removal easier. | Successive ionization energies generally increase for a given element.
Why: Subshell energy and pairing explain the familiar Be/B and N/O exceptions; removing a bound electron costs energy.

questions.title: Paramagnetism of an ion
body: Which isolated ground-state ion is paramagnetic? Use Hund’s rule for the d orbitals. Z: Ca=20, Ti=22, Fe=26, Zn=30.

blocks: C. Fe³⁺
Why: Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵ with five unpaired electrons; the others have closed-shell configurations.

questions.title: Count unpaired d electrons
body: For isolated Co²⁺ (Z=27), which pair correctly gives its condensed configuration and number of unpaired electrons? Assume Hund’s-rule d occupancy.

blocks: A. [Ar]3d⁷; 3
Why: Remove the 4s electrons first, then fill the five degenerate d orbitals by Hund’s rule.

questions.title: Read orbital diagrams
body: The three panels show proposed p⁴ arrangements. Select every correct statement.
choices: Panel B violates the Pauli exclusion principle.
Panel B has all electrons paired but is not the Hund’s-rule ground-state arrangement.
Panel C is forbidden by Pauli exclusion.
Panel A is the Hund’s-rule ground-state arrangement and has 2 unpaired electrons.
An even total electron count always means diamagnetism.

blocks: B, C, D. Panel B has all electrons paired but is not the Hund’s-rule ground-state arrangement. | Panel C is forbidden by Pauli exclusion. | Panel A is the Hund’s-rule ground-state arrangement and has 2 unpaired electrons.
Why: A is [↑↓][↑][↑]; B is prematurely paired; C puts parallel spins into the same orbital.

questions.figureAlt: Three p4 orbital diagrams: A [↑↓][↑][↑], B [↑↓][↑↓][ ], C [↑↑][↑][↑].

questions.title: Find the pair with different configurations
body: Which pair does NOT have identical isolated ground-state electron configurations? Z: Cr=24, Fe=26, Cu=29, Zn=30.

blocks: B. Cr and Fe²⁺
Why: Cr is [Ar]3d⁵4s¹, whereas Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶. Equal electron count is not enough for all open-shell transition-metal comparisons.

questions.title: Configuration exceptions survive careful electron removal
body: Which set is correct? Z(Cu)=29.

blocks: A. Cu [Ar]3d¹⁰4s¹; Cu⁺ [Ar]3d¹⁰; Cu²⁺ [Ar]3d⁹
Why: Neutral Cu is an Aufbau-pattern exception; its highest-n 4s electron is lost before 3d electrons.

questions.title: Choose identical electron configurations
body: Select every pair with identical ground-state configurations. Atomic numbers: Ar18, K19, Ca20, Cr24, Fe26, Cu29, Zn30.

blocks: A, C, E. K⁺ and Ca²⁺ | Ar and S²⁻ | Cu⁺ and Zn²⁺
Why: The first and fourth pairs are [Ar]; Cu⁺ and Zn²⁺ are [Ar]3d¹⁰. Cr versus Fe²⁺ is the important same-electron-count exception.

questions.title: Choose a valid carbonyl Lewis structure
body: The diagram shows four proposed Lewis structures for COCl₂. Which panel satisfies electron count, second-period octets, and the usual lowest-formal-charge preference? Valence electrons: C4, O6, Cl7.

blocks: A. Panel A
Why: A uses 24 electrons, gives every atom an octet, and has zero formal charges. B overfills C; C leaves C short of an octet; D overfills O.

questions.figureAlt: COCl2 candidates with all lone pairs shown. A has C=O and two C-Cl; B also has a C=Cl; C has only single bonds; D has C=O but an extra O lone pair.

questions.title: Choose an octet structure for an ion
body: Which description is the best major Lewis contributor for NO₂⁻? N5, O6 valence electrons.
choices: Two N=O bonds and one lone pair on N.
One N=O, one N–O, one lone pair on N; double O has two lone pairs and single O three.
Two N–O bonds, no lone pair on N, and three lone pairs on each O.
One N=O and one N–O, but no lone pair on N.

blocks: B. One N=O, one N–O, one lone pair on N; double O has two lone pairs and single O three.
Why: 18 total electrons give N one lone pair and an octet with one double and one single bond; the other equivalent form swaps O positions.

questions.title: An incomplete octet can be correct
body: Which is the preferred introductory Lewis description for an isolated BF₃ molecule? B3 and F7 valence electrons.
choices: Three B–F single bonds; no B lone pair; three lone pairs on each F; B has six surrounding electrons.
Three B=F bonds give B an ordinary allowed second-period expanded octet.
Three B–F single bonds and one B lone pair; the neutral molecule has 26 electrons.
One B=F double bond and two B–F single bonds are required because B can never have fewer than eight electrons.

blocks: A. Three B–F single bonds; no B lone pair; three lone pairs on each F; B has six surrounding electrons.
Why: BF₃ is a common electron-deficient exception: 24 total electrons, six around B, with zero formal charges in the single-bond drawing.

questions.title: Infer net charge from every electron pair
body: The drawing shows N=C=O with two lone pairs on N, two on O, and none on C. What is its formula including net charge? N5, C4, O6 valence electrons.
questions.familyTitle: Infer a formula or charge from a drawing

blocks: D. NCO⁻
Why: The drawing contains 16 electrons; the neutral valence sum is 15, so its charge is −1.

questions.figureAlt: N=C=O with two lone pairs on each terminal atom; no central lone pair.

questions.title: A second drawing, a different charge
body: The diagram shows a C center with three O neighbors: one double bond and two single bonds. Double O has two lone pairs; each single O has three. No lone pairs are on C. What species is shown?
questions.familyTitle: Infer a formula or charge from a drawing

blocks: D. CO₃²⁻
Why: The 24 drawn electrons exceed the neutral C+3O sum of 22 by two.

questions.figureAlt: Carbon connected to three oxygens, one double and two single; all terminal lone pairs shown.

questions.title: Check a drawing by two independent methods
body: The same N=C=O drawing has two lone pairs on N and on O. Select every true statement. N5, C4, O6 valence electrons.
choices: The N and O atoms each have an octet.
Its net charge is +1 because N is less electronegative than O.
The formal charges on N, C, O are −1, 0, 0.
questions.familyTitle: Infer a formula or charge from a drawing

blocks: A, B, C, E. The net charge is −1. | The drawing contains 16 valence electrons. | The N and O atoms each have an octet. | The formal charges on N, C, O are −1, 0, 0.
Why: Electron excess and the sum of formal charges independently give charge −1; all three atoms have octets.

questions.figureAlt: N=C=O with two lone pairs on each terminal atom.

questions.title: Formal charge versus oxidation state
body: In a major NO₃⁻ contributor, N has one double bond and two single bonds and no lone pairs. What are N’s formal charge and oxidation number? Take O oxidation number as −2.

blocks: C. FC +1; oxidation number +5
Why: FC = 5 − 4 = +1; charge balance x + 3(−2) = −1 gives oxidation number +5.

questions.title: Assign formal charges from a labeled structure
body: For the depicted O₃ contributor, the terminal double-bonded O has two lone pairs, central O one, and terminal single-bonded O three. What are the formal charges in that order?

blocks: Why: For oxygen, FC = 6 − nonbonding electrons − sum of bond orders.

questions.figureAlt: O=O–O with terminal double O two lone pairs, central O one lone pair, single O three lone pairs.

questions.title: Oxidation-number exceptions and formal charge
body: Select every correct statement.
choices: In H₂O₂, H is +1 and O is −1.
In OF₂, oxygen is −2 because oxygen has no exceptions.
A carbon oxidation number of +4 in CO₂ proves that it contains isolated C⁴⁺ ions.
Formal charges sum to the overall species charge.
In NaH, Na is +1 and H is −1.

blocks: A, D, E. In H₂O₂, H is +1 and O is −1. | Formal charges sum to the overall species charge. | In NaH, Na is +1 and H is −1.
Why: Peroxides and metal hydrides are exceptions; F forces O to +2 in OF₂. Formal charge and oxidation state are bookkeeping conventions.

questions.title: Equivalent nitrate contributors
body: How many equivalent major octet resonance contributors does NO₃⁻ have, and what is its average N–O bond order?

blocks: Why: One N=O can be placed at any of three equivalent oxygen sites; (2+1+1)/3 = 4/3.

questions.title: Nitrite versus nitrate
body: Which comparison is correct? Use equivalent major octet contributors.
choices: NO₂⁻ has 2 contributors and average order 1.5; NO₃⁻ has 3 and average order 4/3.
NO₃⁻ alternates between one short and two long bonds at every instant.
NO₂⁻ has 1 contributor because its O atoms are permanently different.
Both have 3 contributors and average order 4/3.

blocks: A. NO₂⁻ has 2 contributors and average order 1.5; NO₃⁻ has 3 and average order 4/3.
Why: Equivalent oxygen positions produce delocalized real bonds; the hybrid is not a sequence of switching Lewis structures.

questions.title: What resonance does and does not mean
body: Select every true statement.
choices: Atoms retain the same connectivity in resonance forms.
All possible resonance contributors necessarily have equal weights.
A C–O order of 4/3 is an average bonding description, not 4/3 of a localized two-electron pair fixed in one bond.
Equivalent contributors to CO₃²⁻ give equal C–O bond lengths in the actual ion.
A resonance arrow means that the molecule rapidly changes into different compounds.

blocks: A, C, D. Atoms retain the same connectivity in resonance forms. | A C–O order of 4/3 is an average bonding description, not 4/3 of a localized two-electron pair fixed in one bond. | Equivalent contributors to CO₃²⁻ give equal C–O bond lengths in the actual ion.
Why: Electron placement varies between contributors; nuclei/connectivity do not. Unequal contributors should not be averaged with equal weights.

questions.title: Shape from a supplied Lewis pattern
body: In ClO₃F, a supplied Lewis contributor has Cl bonded to three O atoms by double bonds and to F by a single bond, with no Cl lone pair. What is the molecular geometry at Cl?

blocks: D. Tetrahedral
Why: Four neighboring atoms give four domains; multiple bonds each count once. Four bonds and no lone pairs give AX₄.

questions.title: Five domains, four bonded atoms
body: SF₄ has 34 valence electrons. After S–F bonds and F octets are filled, one lone pair remains on S. What are its electron geometry and molecular shape?

blocks: B. Trigonal bipyramidal; seesaw
Why: Four bonds plus one lone pair give five domains; the lone pair is equatorial.

questions.title: Lone-pair variants of six domains
body: Select every correct geometry assignment.
choices: XeF₄: octahedral electron geometry, square-planar molecular shape.
SF₆: octahedral electron and molecular geometries.
BrF₅: octahedral electron geometry, square-pyramidal molecular shape.
ClF₃: trigonal-bipyramidal electron geometry, T-shaped molecular shape.
XeF₂: tetrahedral electron geometry, bent molecular shape.

blocks: A, B, C, D. XeF₄: octahedral electron geometry, square-planar molecular shape. | SF₆: octahedral electron and molecular geometries. | BrF₅: octahedral electron geometry, square-pyramidal molecular shape. | ClF₃: trigonal-bipyramidal electron geometry, T-shaped molecular shape.
Why: Count central lone pairs as well as bonds: XeF₂ has five domains and is linear, not bent.

questions.title: A two-bond anion need not be linear
body: PH₂⁻ has P as the center. P has 5 and H 1 valence electron. Which prediction follows the lecture VSEPR model?

blocks: C. Bent; H–P–H <109.5°
Why: 5+2+1=8 electrons; two bonds leave two lone pairs on P. AX₂E₂ has tetrahedral electron geometry and a bent shape.

questions.title: A double bond distorts a planar center
body: For O=CCl₂ with no central lone pair, which angle comparison is predicted by simple VSEPR?

blocks: B. Cl–C–Cl <120° and O–C–Cl >120°
Why: The double-bond domain repels adjacent single-bond domains more strongly and compresses the angle between those single bonds.

questions.title: Angle reasoning across familiar molecules
body: Select every statement consistent with the introductory VSEPR model.
choices: All sp³ centers must have an experimental angle of exactly 109.5°.
CH₄ has ideal H–C–H angles of 109.5°.
The two bonds in CO₂ count as four domains because they are double bonds.
Lone pairs prefer equatorial positions in a trigonal-bipyramidal arrangement.
NH₃ and H₂O have tetrahedral electron geometry but smaller bond angles than CH₄.

blocks: B, D, E. CH₄ has ideal H–C–H angles of 109.5°. | Lone pairs prefer equatorial positions in a trigonal-bipyramidal arrangement. | NH₃ and H₂O have tetrahedral electron geometry but smaller bond angles than CH₄.
Why: Domain geometry gives ideal angles; lone pairs and unequal bonding domains produce distortions.

questions.title: Hybridization of a charged central atom
body: For SnCl₃⁻, use Sn4 and Cl7 valence electrons and the lecture localized model. Which description is correct at Sn?
choices: sp³; one lone pair; trigonal pyramidal
sp²; zero lone pairs; trigonal planar

blocks: A. sp³; one lone pair; trigonal pyramidal
Why: 4+21+1=26 electrons. Three bonds and Cl octets leave one Sn lone pair: four domains.

questions.title: Four bonds can require six hybrid directions
body: Which pair of lecture-model hybridizations is correct for PCl₄⁺ and XeF₄? P5, Cl7, Xe8, F7 valence electrons.
choices: Both sp³ because each has four bonded atoms

blocks: B. PCl₄⁺ sp³; XeF₄ sp³d²
Why: PCl₄⁺ has four bonds/no lone pair; XeF₄ has four bonds/two lone pairs. The d-containing label is the course’s simplified model.

questions.title: Hybridization bookkeeping for ions
body: Select every correct lecture-model assignment.
choices: BF₄⁻: B is sp² because neutral BF₃ is sp².

blocks: A, B, C, E. NO₂⁻: N is sp². | ClF₃: Cl is sp³d. | NH₄⁺: N is sp³. | I₃⁻: central I is sp³d.
Why: Use the actual charged species: BF₄⁻ has four domains, so it is sp³. I₃⁻ and ClF₃ each have five domains.

questions.title: Read a labeled carbon in a structure
body: In the labeled molecule, which hybridization describes C5? Use the localized lecture model.

blocks: A. sp
Why: The nitrile carbon has two neighbors and two σ-domain directions despite its triple bond.

questions.figureAlt: CH₂(C1)=CH(C2)–C3(=O)–CH₂(C4)–C5≡N, with all carbon labels visible.

questions.title: Read two different local environments
body: For the same labeled molecule, what are the hybridizations of C3 and C4, respectively?

blocks: D. sp²; sp³
Why: The carbonyl carbon has three domains; the methylene carbon has four.

questions.figureAlt: CH₂(C1)=CH(C2)–C3(=O)–CH₂(C4)–C5≡N.

questions.title: Hybrid orbitals versus p orbitals
body: For the labeled molecule, select every true statement in the localized model.
choices: C4 is sp³ and contributes no unhybridized valence p orbital to a localized π bond.
The π part of C1=C2 forms through end-to-end overlap of sp² hybrids.
C5 retains two unhybridized p orbitals for π bonding.
C1 retains one unhybridized p orbital for π bonding.
The C3–C4 σ bond can be described as sp²–sp³ overlap.

blocks: A, C, D, E. C4 is sp³ and contributes no unhybridized valence p orbital to a localized π bond. | C5 retains two unhybridized p orbitals for π bonding. | C1 retains one unhybridized p orbital for π bonding. | The C3–C4 σ bond can be described as sp²–sp³ overlap.
Why: Hybrids describe the σ framework; parallel unhybridized p orbitals supply π overlap.

questions.figureAlt: CH₂(C1)=CH(C2)–C3(=O)–CH₂(C4)–C5≡N.

questions.title: Rank electronegativity with a less familiar metal
body: Which order is decreasing electronegativity? Use the main-group trend.

blocks: B. F > S > Si > Ba
Why: Electronegativity generally increases up and right; S is to the right of Si.

questions.title: Bond polarity and ionic character
body: Data: EN(H)=2.1, C=2.5, N=3.0, O=3.5. Which is decreasing bond polarity (and approximate ionic character)?
choices: All are equally polar because H is present

blocks: A. O–H > N–H > C–H
Why: Compare ΔEN: 1.4, 0.9, 0.4. This also corrects the reversed printed inequality in slide 42.

questions.title: Separate electronegativity from ionization energy
body: Select every true statement.
choices: A molecule with at least one polar bond must have a nonzero net dipole.
Electronegativity describes attraction for shared bonding electrons.
In N–F, electron density is drawn toward F.
In O–H, H is δ⁺ and O is δ⁻.
Ionization energy is the energy change for adding an electron to a gaseous atom.

blocks: B, C, D. Electronegativity describes attraction for shared bonding electrons. | In N–F, electron density is drawn toward F. | In O–H, H is δ⁺ and O is δ⁻.
Why: Molecular geometry determines cancellation. Ionization energy concerns removal; electron affinity concerns addition.

questions.title: Choose the zero-dipole molecule
body: Which isolated molecule has zero net dipole?

blocks: D. XeF₄
Why: Opposite lone pairs leave a symmetric square-planar array of identical F ligands in XeF₄.

questions.title: All the nonpolar cases
body: Select every nonpolar molecule in its usual isolated geometry.

blocks: A, B, C, D. CO₂ | XeF₂ | BF₃ | SF₆
Why: Identical symmetric bond dipoles cancel in the first four; the two different ends of COS do not cancel.

questions.title: Symmetry of two planar isomers
body: The diagram shows cis- and trans-1,2-dichloroethene. Which pair correctly identifies their net dipoles?
choices: both zero because both contain the same bonds
both nonzero because C–Cl bonds are polar

blocks: C. cis nonzero; trans zero
Why: The symmetric opposite C–Cl dipoles cancel in trans but reinforce in cis.

questions.figureAlt: Two planar CHCl=CHCl drawings: cis has both Cl on the same side; trans has Cl on opposite sides.

questions.title: Shape and polarity of a mixed-ligand center
body: Which description of CH₂Cl₂ is correct?

blocks: D. Tetrahedral and polar
Why: Four domains around carbon give tetrahedral geometry; unlike ligand sets prevent complete dipole cancellation.

questions.title: A shape name alone does not settle polarity
body: Which comparison is correct?
choices: CHCl₃ is trigonal pyramidal because it has three Cl atoms.
Both must be polar because both contain C–Cl bonds.
CCl₄ and CHCl₃ are both tetrahedral, but only CHCl₃ is polar.
Both are square planar and nonpolar.

blocks: C. CCl₄ and CHCl₃ are both tetrahedral, but only CHCl₃ is polar.
Why: Count all four neighboring atoms, then compare vector cancellation rather than counting only one ligand type.

questions.title: Choose the correct shape-polarity pairs
body: Select every correct pair.

blocks: A, B, D. PCl₅: trigonal bipyramidal, nonpolar. | XeF₂: linear, nonpolar. | BrF₅: square pyramidal, polar.
Why: Count central lone pairs: SF₄ is seesaw; NH₃ is trigonal pyramidal.

questions.title: Count bonds in a ring with a nitrile substituent
body: The drawing is benzonitrile: a six-membered carbon ring with three alternating double bonds, five ring hydrogens, and one –C≡N substituent. How many σ and π bonds are present?
questions.familyTitle: Sigma and pi counts in molecular drawings

blocks: Why: σ: six ring links + five C–H + one ring–C + one C–N = 13. π: three ring + two nitrile = 5.

questions.figureAlt: Explicit alternating-bond benzene ring with five H atoms and a C≡N substituent.

questions.title: Two oxygen-containing aromatic drawings
body: The diagram labels phenol A and anisole B. Which total σ/π counts are correct? All C–H and O–H bonds count.
questions.familyTitle: Sigma and pi counts in molecular drawings

blocks: Why: Phenol has 6 ring + 5 ring C–H + C–O + O–H. Anisole replaces O–H by O–C plus three C–H.

questions.figureAlt: A is phenol C₆H₅–O–H; B is anisole C₆H₅–O–CH₃; ring alternating double bonds are explicit.

questions.title: Audit a styrene bond count
body: For styrene C₆H₅–CH=CH₂, drawn with three alternating ring double bonds, select every correct statement.
choices: The exocyclic C=C bond contains one σ and one π.
Both carbons of the –CH=CH₂ group are sp².
There are 16 σ bonds in the whole molecule.
The ring has three σ and three π bonds total.
questions.familyTitle: Sigma and pi counts in molecular drawings

blocks: A, B, C, D. The exocyclic C=C bond contains one σ and one π. | Both carbons of the –CH=CH₂ group are sp². | There are 16 σ bonds in the whole molecule. | There are 4 π bonds.
Why: The six-membered ring has six σ bonds, not three; include all eight C–H bonds and both side-chain C–C connections.

questions.figureAlt: Benzene ring with three alternating double bonds and –CH=CH₂ substituent.

questions.title: Normal boiling point from one pressure
body: Data: R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹; T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15; normal boiling pressure = 760 torr. Treat ΔHvap as constant.
A liquid has vapor pressure 180.0 torr at 298.0 K and ΔHvap = 32.00 kJ/mol. What is its normal boiling point?

questions.title: Predict a new vapor pressure
body: Data: R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹; T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15; normal boiling pressure = 760 torr. Treat ΔHvap as constant.
A liquid has vapor pressure 100.0 torr at 300.0 K and ΔHvap = 30.00 kJ/mol. What is its pressure at 320.0 K?

blocks: A. 212 torr
Why: ln(P₂/100) = (30000/R)(1/300 − 1/320); exponentiate to obtain about 212 torr.

questions.title: Infer ΔHvap before predicting behavior
body: Data: R = 8.314 J·mol⁻¹·K⁻¹; T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15; normal boiling pressure = 760 torr. Treat ΔHvap as constant.
A liquid has vapor pressure 80.00 torr at 298.15 K and 240.0 torr at 323.15 K. Which estimate of ΔHvap is correct?

blocks: D. 35.2 kJ/mol
Why: ΔHvap = R ln(240/80)/(1/298.15 − 1/323.15) = 35.2 kJ/mol; use Kelvin and J-to-kJ conversion.

questions.title: Compare similar-mass molecular liquids
body: Which has the highest normal boiling point: propane (44.10 g/mol), dimethyl ether (46.07), or ethanol (46.07)?
choices: All equal because their masses are similar

blocks: B. Ethanol
Why: Ethanol can hydrogen-bond to itself; ether has no O–H donor, and propane is nonpolar.

questions.title: Large nonpolar clouds versus small dipoles
body: I₂ is nonpolar and boils at a much higher temperature than polar HCl. Which explanation is best?
choices: I₂ must form hydrogen bonds because its boiling point is high.
I₂ has a much larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so its dispersion attractions can outweigh those in small HCl.
Every nonpolar substance has stronger attractions than every polar one.

blocks: C. I₂ has a much larger, more polarizable electron cloud, so its dispersion attractions can outweigh those in small HCl.
Why: IMF comparisons require size/polarizability as well as named force categories; there is no universal category-only ranking.

questions.title: Shape and polarizability change boiling point
body: Select every correct prediction or explanation.
choices: A molecule with a permanent dipole always boils higher than every nonpolar molecule.
Boiling ethanol normally breaks its C–O covalent bonds.
For otherwise similar molecules, stronger attractions generally raise boiling point.
n-Pentane boils higher than compact neopentane because its shape allows greater intermolecular contact.
Br₂ boils higher than Cl₂ because it is generally more polarizable.

blocks: C, D, E. For otherwise similar molecules, stronger attractions generally raise boiling point. | n-Pentane boils higher than compact neopentane because its shape allows greater intermolecular contact. | Br₂ boils higher than Cl₂ because it is generally more polarizable.
Why: Contact area and polarizability affect attractions; boiling changes intermolecular organization rather than ordinary covalent connectivity.

questions.title: Compare vapor pressures at one temperature
body: At the same temperature, compare hypothetical liquid samples of CH₃OH, CH₃OCH₃, and CH₃CH₂CH₃, each with equilibrium vapor pressure. Which has the lowest vapor pressure?
choices: All are equal at the same temperature

blocks: A. CH₃OH
Why: Among these similar-mass molecules, methanol’s hydrogen bonding gives the strongest attraction and lowest vapor pressure.

questions.title: Read vapor-pressure curves
body: The graph shows two pure-liquid vapor-pressure curves and a 760-torr line. Select every true statement over the displayed range.
choices: B’s normal boiling point is 340 K.
A has the lower normal boiling point.
At 320 K, A has the higher vapor pressure.
A necessarily has the stronger intermolecular attractions because its vapor pressure is higher.
The normal boiling points occur where each curve meets 760 torr.

blocks: A, B, C, E. B’s normal boiling point is 340 K. | A has the lower normal boiling point. | At 320 K, A has the higher vapor pressure. | The normal boiling points occur where each curve meets 760 torr.
Why: A reaches 760 torr at 320 K; B at 340 K. Higher vapor pressure at the same T generally indicates easier escape.

questions.figureAlt: Curve A crosses 760 torr at 320 K; curve B crosses at 340 K. A lies above B at a common temperature.

questions.title: External pressure versus saturation vapor pressure
body: A pure liquid at 30°C is moved to a lower-pressure environment, while its temperature is held at 30°C and liquid remains. Which statement is correct?
choices: Its equilibrium vapor pressure at 30°C is unchanged, but its boiling temperature at the lower external pressure is lower.
Its equilibrium vapor pressure equals the new external pressure at every temperature.
Its intermolecular forces become stronger when external pressure falls.
Both equilibrium vapor pressure and normal boiling point must decrease.

blocks: A. Its equilibrium vapor pressure at 30°C is unchanged, but its boiling temperature at the lower external pressure is lower.
Why: Saturation vapor pressure is a function of substance and T; boiling requires matching external pressure.

questions.title: Hydrogen bonding in a pure sample
body: Which pair can each hydrogen-bond to identical molecules in a pure sample?

blocks: C. CH₃OH and CH₃NH₂
Why: Each member needs an appropriate N–H, O–H, or F–H donor plus a suitable acceptor in this introductory model.

questions.title: Donors and acceptors are different roles
body: Select every true statement using the introductory course H-bond model.
choices: CH₃OCH₃ can accept a hydrogen bond from water.
CH₃OH both donates and accepts hydrogen bonds.
CH₃OCH₃ hydrogen-bonds to identical ether molecules because it contains O.
CH₃F is treated as a conventional self-hydrogen-bonding liquid merely because it contains both H and F.

blocks: A, B, E. CH₃OCH₃ can accept a hydrogen bond from water. | CH₃OH both donates and accepts hydrogen bonds. | CH₃NH₂ can hydrogen-bond to itself.
Why: Ether has O lone pairs but no appropriate donor H; carbon-bound H in CH₃F is not H–F.

questions.title: List all forces, not only the strongest
body: Which list gives all major intermolecular force types present in pure liquid methanol?
choices: Dispersion only because the whole molecule is neutral

blocks: A. Dispersion, dipole–dipole, and hydrogen bonding
Why: Every molecule has dispersion; polar methanol also has dipole–dipole attractions and O–H hydrogen bonding.

questions.title: Matter wavelength without a long calculation chain
body: An electron (m = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moves at 1.00 × 10⁶ m/s. Which gives its de Broglie wavelength and the effect of doubling its speed?

blocks: D. 0.727 nm; wavelength halves
Why: λ = h/(mv) = 7.27 × 10⁻¹⁰ m. Wavelength is inversely proportional to momentum.

questions.title: Uncertainty and relative precision
body: Use Δx·mΔv ≥ h/(4π). An electron has speed 2.00 × 10⁶ m/s with uncertainty Δv = 0.800% of that speed; m = 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg. What is the minimum Δx, and how does it change if Δv is reduced by a factor of 4?

blocks: C. 3.62 nm; minimum Δx increases by 4
Why: Δv = 1.60 × 10⁴ m/s. The uncertainty-product bound makes the minimum Δx inversely proportional to Δv.

questions.title: Orbitals, nodes, shielding, and penetration
body: Select every correct statement in the course atomic model.
choices: Inner electrons effectively shield outer electrons from the full nuclear charge.
For a typical multielectron atom at fixed n, s generally lies below p because of greater penetration.
The two lobes of one p orbital are two separate orbitals.
For isolated H, 3s, 3p, and 3d are degenerate in the model.

blocks: A, B, C, E. A 4s orbital has 3 total nodes. | Inner electrons effectively shield outer electrons from the full nuclear charge. | For a typical multielectron atom at fixed n, s generally lies below p because of greater penetration. | For isolated H, 3s, 3p, and 3d are degenerate in the model.
Why: Total nodes = n−1. Shielding/penetration split same-n subshell energies in multielectron atoms.

questions.title: Inert-pair and pseudo-noble-gas configurations
body: Sn has [Kr]4d¹⁰5s²5p². Which comparison is correct?
choices: Both ions are isoelectronic with Xe.
Sn²⁺ is [Kr]4d¹⁰5s² (inert pair); Sn⁴⁺ is [Kr]4d¹⁰ (pseudo-noble gas).
Sn²⁺ has two unpaired 5p electrons and must be paramagnetic.

blocks: B. Sn²⁺ is [Kr]4d¹⁰5s² (inert pair); Sn⁴⁺ is [Kr]4d¹⁰ (pseudo-noble gas).
Why: Remove highest-n p electrons first, then s. The retained 5s² pair and filled d¹⁰ configuration have distinct lecture names.

questions.title: Electron-affinity signs and a familiar exception
body: Use signed electron affinities for X(g)+e⁻→X⁻(g): EA(F)=−328, EA(Cl)=−349 kJ/mol. Select every correct statement.
choices: Adding an electron to Cl releases more energy than adding one to F.
The data prove that EA becomes steadily more negative going upward in every group.
Adding a second electron to O⁻(g) ordinarily requires energy.
The more negative EA is the more exothermic addition.
IE and EA are the same process with the same sign.

blocks: A, C, D. Adding an electron to Cl releases more energy than adding one to F. | Adding a second electron to O⁻(g) ordinarily requires energy. | The more negative EA is the more exothermic addition.
Why: EA trends have exceptions; gas-phase addition to an already negative ion opposes electrostatic repulsion.

questions.title: Covalent radius versus nonbonded contact
body: The Cl–Cl covalent bond length is 198 pm; closest nonbonded Cl···Cl contact is 360 pm. An additive covalent-radius model gives C–Cl = 176 pm. Which set is correct?
choices: r covalent(Cl)=99 pm; r vdW(Cl)=180 pm; r covalent(C)=77 pm

blocks: C. r covalent(Cl)=99 pm; r vdW(Cl)=180 pm; r covalent(C)=77 pm
Why: Each identical-atom distance is twice the corresponding radius. Use covalent, not van der Waals, radius in the C–Cl bond estimate.

questions.title: Light and quantum-model evidence
body: Select every true statement.
choices: An orbital specifies a definite circular electron path.
Planck’s oscillator model permits energy changes in integer multiples of hν.
Higher amplitude can raise light intensity without changing its frequency.
Radio has higher photon energy than ultraviolet.

blocks: B, C, F. Planck’s oscillator model permits energy changes in integer multiples of hν. | Higher amplitude can raise light intensity without changing its frequency. | Diffraction demonstrates wave behavior.
Why: Wave interference/diffraction and quantized energy exchange are complementary evidence; E varies inversely with wavelength.

questions.title: Bonding models and conductivity
body: Select every correct statement about pure Cu, NaCl, and CH₃OH.
choices: Cu has metallic bonding and mobile electrons that carry current.
Molten NaCl can conduct because ions are mobile.
CH₃OH has covalent bonds within molecules and intermolecular attractions between them.
Solid NaCl conducts well because its ions are charged even when fixed.
An ionic crystal can fracture when displacement places like charges next to one another.

blocks: A, B, C, E. Cu has metallic bonding and mobile electrons that carry current. | Molten NaCl can conduct because ions are mobile. | CH₃OH has covalent bonds within molecules and intermolecular attractions between them. | An ionic crystal can fracture when displacement places like charges next to one another.
Why: Charge carriers must be mobile. Ionic solids are extended lattices, whereas methanol consists of covalent molecules.

questions.title: Lattice attraction: charge and separation

questions.title: Bond order, length, and strength

blocks: A. Length: C≡C < C=C < C–C; higher bond order generally means a stronger bond.
Why: Additional bonding generally increases attraction and shortens a comparable bond; π and σ components are not identical in strength.

blocks: B. A contributes more; an unweighted bond-order average is not exact.

answer.text:

    """Insert a character into an ascending string without sorting."""
    i = 0
    while i < len(text) and text[i] <= char:
        i += 1
    return text[:i] + char + text[i:]

def myinsert2(values, value):
    """Return a new ascending list with value inserted, without sorting."""
    i = 0
    while i < len(values) and values[i] <= value:
        i += 1
    return values[:i] + [value] + values[i:]'}]

from math import pi, sqrt, exp
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def normal_values(mu, sigma, xs):
    """Return normal-density values; sigma must be positive."""
    if sigma <= 0:
        raise ValueError("sigma must be positive")
    result = []
    for x in xs:
        result.append(exp(-(x - mu) ** 2 / (2 * sigma ** 2)) / sqrt(2 * pi * sigma ** 2))
    return result

xs = [i / 20 for i in range(-80, 81)]
ys = normal_values(0, 1, xs)
plt.plot(xs, ys)
plt.xlabel("x")
plt.ylabel("P(x)")
plt.title("Normal probability density")
plt.show()

from math import factorial

def tay_term(n, x):
    """Return term n of the Maclaurin series for cos(x), in radians."""
    return (-1) ** n * x ** (2 * n) / factorial(2 * n)

x = float(input("Enter a value for x: "))

n = 0
while True:
    term = tay_term(n, x)
    total += term
    if abs(term) < 1e-7:
        break
    n += 1
print(f"The cosine of {x} is {total:.7f}")

n = int(input("Enter the number of students: "))

sections.title: Purpose
body: Compare glassware, prepare a NaCl solution, and identify an unknown by combining conductivity with density. Calculate each density from liquid mass and measured volume before comparing replicate results.

figures.alt: Beaker, Erlenmeyer flask, volumetric flask, and graduated cylinder
figures.author: Community College Consortium of Bioscience Credentials

figures.alt: Volumetric pipet with a central bulb
figures.author: Zelda F. Scott

figures.alt: Clear rectangular cuvette being filled with a transfer pipet
figures.author: KhomchatK

sections.title: What the glassware is for
body: A beaker has a spout and rough marks. Use it for holding and mixing. A narrow-necked Erlenmeyer lets you swirl with less splashing. A graduated cylinder has multiple graduations for measuring variable volumes. A capped vial holds small samples. Its capacity is not a calibrated volume.

sections.title: Containing versus delivering
body: A volumetric flask has one mark and sets the final solution volume. A bulb volumetric pipet has one mark for delivering a fixed aliquot. A squeeze transfer pipet moves drops or rough amounts. A cuvette is the rectangular optical sample holder. identify its clear faces.

sections.title: Reading instruments
body: Read a water meniscus at eye level at its lowest point. Estimate one digit beyond the smallest readable analog division, such as 22.21 mL with 0.1 mL markings. Digital instruments give the displayed digits. The lab balance reads to 0.0001 g. Follow the instrument's actual scale or stated tolerance for a specific item. Glassware type alone does not dictate decimal places.

sections.title: Significant figures
body: Leading zeros are placeholders, zeros between nonzero digits count, and terminal zeros after a decimal count. For addition/subtraction, round by decimal place. For multiplication/division, round by the limiting significant figures. Keep guard digits and round once at the end. Exact unit conversions do not limit sig figs.

sections.title: Density and molarity
body: Density = (filled mass − empty mass)/liquid volume. Use the same container and tare conditions. Molarity = (mass of solute / molar mass) / final solution volume in L. Overshooting the flask mark makes the actual solution dilute. Loss of solute in transfer also lowers actual concentration.

sections.title: Conductivity and unknowns
body: Dissolved mobile ions carry charge, so adding NaCl to distilled water generally raises conductivity. A film on the probe can delay return to the air baseline and carry salt into the next sample. Compare conductivity and density together. Density alone may confuse 95% ethanol with a salt/methanol mixture.

sections.title: Safety and data quality
body: Use splash goggles and a pipet bulb. Keep balance doors closed for a stable reading and retain the last reported digit. Use the course's disposal instructions for the unknown. Repeated values show precision. comparison against a reference is needed to assess accuracy.

sections.title: What happened in the lab
body: First, you mixed a measured portion of the unknown CuSO₄ solution with sodium carbonate. A solid formed. You collected it on preweighed filter paper, dried it on a watch glass, let it cool, and weighed the paper plus solid. Subtracting the paper mass gave the mass of precipitate. From that mass and the reaction's mole ratio, you calculated how much CuSO₄ was in the original portion.

Then you used a fresh portion of the same unknown for a light-based measurement. You prepared three standards by successively halving a known CuSO₄ stock, giving 50%, 25%, and 12.5% of the stock concentration. After blanking the spectrophotometer with reverse-osmosis water, you scanned the stock to find its peak wavelength and measured the stock, standards, and unknown at that wavelength.

Finally, you plotted absorbance against concentration for the known solutions and used the unknown's absorbance to read its concentration from the fit. You compared that value with the one calculated from the precipitate mass.

sections.title: Purpose
body: Estimate unknown CuSO₄ molarity by mass of a precipitate and by visible-light absorbance. Both methods report the original concentration but rely on different signals.

sections.title: Gravimetric workflow
body: Use the course model CuSO₄(aq) + Na₂CO₃(aq) → CuCO₃(s) + Na₂SO₄(aq). Compare initial moles to check that carbonate is in excess. Subtract filter tare as appropriate, convert dry CuCO₃ mass to moles, apply the 1:1 ratio, and divide by the original sample volume in liters. Residual water raises mass. solid lost during filtering lowers it.

sections.title: Prepare and measure standards
body: Use C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ for dilution. For sequential dilutions, the new solution becomes the next stock. Blank with the prescribed reference. Wipe the clear faces of the cuvette, avoid bubbles in the beam, and keep orientation and path length consistent.

sections.title: Two plots with different jobs
body: An absorbance spectrum plots A vs wavelength. Its peak defines λmax. measuring near it can give a strong concentration response. A calibration curve plots A vs known concentration at one wavelength. Use c = (A − intercept)/slope, then undo any unknown dilution.

sections.title: Light and concentration
body: T = I/I₀, %T = 100T, and A = −log₁₀(T). In the linear region, A = εbc. At very low concentrations, changes can be small compared with noise. High concentrations can depart from the line. Dilute an overly concentrated unknown and use interpolation.

sections.title: Compare methods
body: Closely matching results show agreement, but a known reference or recovery check is needed to judge accuracy. Errors can cancel. A smudge that blocks light only for the unknown gives a falsely high absorbance and concentration. An absorbing blank used only on the unknown can do the reverse.

figures.alt: Clear rectangular cuvette being filled with a transfer pipet
figures.author: KhomchatK

sections.title: Equipment and waste
body: Identify the funnel and filter paper for isolating the solid, the volumetric glassware for standards, and the spectrophotometer with its cuvette. Follow the course's chemical waste route for copper-containing mixtures and solid residues.

sections.title: What happened in the lab
body: First, you checked a stoppered flask and its tubing for leaks. You placed the flask in a hot water bath and sealed the air sample once the bath reached boiling. As the bath cooled toward 0 °C, you recorded the pressure inside the flask and the bath temperature once the readings stabilized. The flask kept gas volume fixed, and the seal kept the amount of air fixed.

Next, you connected an air-filled syringe directly to the pressure sensor. You moved the plunger to different volume marks and held it still until the pressure stabilized. The amount of air stayed fixed, and the measurements were taken near room temperature. Smaller syringe volumes gave higher pressures.

In the post-lab, you used the flask data to compare pressure with absolute temperature and extrapolated the Celsius plot to zero pressure. For the syringe data, you plotted both pressure and reciprocal pressure against volume to see which graph gave a straight line.

sections.title: Purpose
body: Use a pressure probe with a temperature bath or syringe, determine which plot is linear, and explain the result with molecular motion.

sections.title: Pressure versus temperature
body: With V and n fixed, P/T is constant and T must be in K for ratios. Plot absolute P versus T(K) for the direct relation. P versus T(°C) is also linear, but its x-intercept estimates absolute zero. For P = mT + b, that intercept is −b/m. A constant positive pressure offset moves it more negative if the fitted slope stays fixed.

sections.title: Pressure versus volume
body: At fixed T and n, PV = constant. P vs V is a decreasing curve. 1/P vs V is linear with slope 1/(nRT) when units are consistent. To predict V at a given pressure, substitute 1/P into the fitted equation.

sections.title: Molecular explanation
body: Heating increases average kinetic energy and raises wall collision frequency and momentum transfer per collision. Isothermal compression keeps average kinetic energy fixed but increases the rate of impacts against walls.

sections.title: Recognize nonideal-looking data
body: Gas or bath temperature can lag the reading used as the x-axis. Fast compression may momentarily heat the gas, so wait for equilibrium. Gas escaping reduces n. tubing adds volume the syringe graduations omit. Extra constant volume produces a positive intercept in 1/P vs indicated syringe V.

sections.title: Graph checks and equipment
body: Label axes and slope units. A best-fit prediction at 200 °C or 10 kPa may be extrapolation, depending on the measured range. Identify the pressure sensor, temperature probe, water bath, and syringe. Follow the lab setup instructions when handling the bath and connected vessel. Air and nitrogen have the same ideal pressure when total moles, V, and T match.

sections.title: What happened in the lab
body: You first made a blue silver nanoparticle dispersion as a baseline. Silver ions were reduced to silver metal, which formed tiny particles suspended in water. You watched the color develop and used a water-blanked spectrophotometer to record the baseline absorbance spectrum and its peak wavelength.

Next, you made more dispersions to test how a growth condition affected the color. The manual allowed changes to citrate, bromide, or peroxide while keeping the amounts of silver nitrate and reducing agent fixed. The supplied post-lab varied bromide and kept the other reagent amounts fixed.

You recorded each vial's stable color, scanned each sample in its own labeled cuvette, and compared the spectra on one graph. The lab aimed for four distinct colors including the baseline, with peak wavelengths at least 15 nm apart. The post-lab then asked whether the changes in peak wavelength actually supported your hypothesis.

sections.title: Purpose
body: Link an intentionally varied synthesis condition to a measured spectrum and observed solution color. Identify the control condition and record all quantities, times, colors, and peak measurements consistently.

sections.title: Particle model and reagents
body: Reduction changes Ag⁺ to Ag⁰. Silver nitrate supplies silver ions, borohydride serves as the reducing agent, and citrate helps stabilize particle surfaces. Peroxide and bromide help control growth and affect the final particle population. Distinguish individual ions, nanoscale clusters suspended in water, and one continuous piece of bulk metal.

sections.title: Why the color changes
body: Light can drive collective oscillation of the mobile electrons in a silver nanoparticle, called localized surface plasmon resonance. Size, shape, aggregation, and the surrounding medium affect the spectrum. What you see depends on transmitted and scattered light. The most absorbed wavelength need not match the visible color.

sections.title: Read the full spectrum
body: Plot absorbance on y and wavelength in nm on x. Label λmax, peak height and width. A shift is a change on the wavelength axis. For unchanged particles and optical path length in the linear range, increasing concentration scales absorbance with little effect on λmax. A broad peak or multiple peaks could arise from a mixture, multiple modes, or aggregation.

sections.title: Interpret a hypothesis
body: Vary one factor and hold the others constant, including measurement timing and cuvette handling. Repeat promising and odd conditions. A broad apparent peak could reflect aggregation or an optical issue. An apparent trend with exceptions does not support an all-trials claim, and λmax alone cannot uniquely determine size.

sections.title: Equipment and waste
body: Recognize the small-volume pipet, vial, cuvette, and spectrophotometer. Read µL separately from mL (1000 µL = 1 mL). Handle cuvettes by the nonoptical faces. Follow the manual and instructor for the silver-containing waste and for the reactive reagents.

sections.title: What happened in the lab
body: First, you mixed measured amounts of hot and cold water in a foam-cup calorimeter and recorded how the temperature changed. You calculated how much heat the hot water lost and the cold water gained. The difference was attributed to the cup. You repeated the calibration three times and averaged the cup constants.

Then you ran two separate reactions in the calibrated cup. One combined magnesium metal with hydrochloric acid and released hydrogen gas. The other combined magnesium oxide with hydrochloric acid and formed water. For each run you used the temperature rise to calculate heat absorbed by the solution and the cup, then converted the reaction heat to kJ per mole of the solid reacted.

Finally, you reversed the magnesium oxide reaction on paper and added it to the magnesium reaction. This canceled the shared acid and dissolved magnesium chloride terms and gave the enthalpy for magnesium metal reacting with water to produce magnesium oxide and hydrogen. You compared that indirect result with the post-lab reference of −315.9 kJ/mol.

sections.title: Purpose
body: Calibrate the cup by mixing hot and cold water, measure q for Mg and MgO reacting with acid, and combine the molar reaction enthalpies with Hess’s law.

sections.title: System and surroundings
body: The reaction is the system. solution and cup are the measured surroundings. ΔT = Tfinal − Tinitial. qsolution = msolution cΔT and qcup = CcalΔT. When the surroundings warm, the reaction releases heat and qrxn is negative. Average the trial calorimeter constants using the course method.

sections.title: Cup calibration
body: If the cup starts at the cold-water temperature, qhot + qcold + qcup = 0, so Ccal = −(qhot + qcold)/(Tf − Tcold). qhot should be negative and qcold positive. A separate heat leak into the room would be wrongly assigned to the cup by this model.

sections.title: Molar reaction enthalpy
body: Use qrxn = −(msolution c + Ccal)ΔT. Convert J to kJ then divide by the moles reacted corresponding to the equation. Check the limiting reagent when acid is not in excess. For Mg and MgO use their own molar masses. Keep kJ/mol separate from total kJ.

sections.title: Hess’s law
body: Keep Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂. Reverse MgO + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂O and flip its enthalpy. Sum to get Mg + H₂O → MgO + H₂. Thus ΔHtarget = ΔHMg − ΔHMgO. If both trials have error, trace each term through its sign before predicting the net effect.

sections.title: Troubleshooting and comparison
body: Heat loss, delayed probe response, or incomplete reaction can make the recorded rise too small. A larger cup heat capacity can lower ΔT without any heat leak. Review the temperature-time trace for a peak and cooling. Absolute percent error = absolute difference divided by the magnitude of the reference, times 100%. Formation data use specified phases. average bond enthalpies refer to gas-phase bonds.

guides.title: Functions of several variables
body: Domain: impose every restriction simultaneously. Square roots require a nonnegative radicand; logarithms require a positive argument; denominators cannot be zero.
Use solid boundaries for included points and dashed boundaries for excluded points. Keep the original restrictions when squaring or solving for a level.
The range is the set of attained output values. Check endpoints rather than assuming they are included.
Level curves satisfy \(f(x,y)=k\); level surfaces satisfy \(f(x,y,z)=k\). They live in input space. Vertical traces use \(x=a\) or \(y=b\).
For equal height steps, closer contours indicate steeper change. Check the labels and scale.

guides.title: Brief continuity review
body: Continuity at \((a,b)\) requires \(\lim_{(x,y)\to(a,b)}f(x,y)=f(a,b)\), through every path in the domain.
Two paths with different limits prove that the limit does not exist. Agreement along a few paths does not prove that a limit exists.
For continuous elementary functions, substitute directly where the expression is defined.
Partial derivatives can exist even when the function is not continuous; see question 14.3.8.

guides.title: Partial derivatives
body: Hold the other variables constant and apply the usual product, quotient, and chain rules.
\(f_x\) and \(f_y\) are coordinate trace slopes, not function heights.
\(f_{xy}=(f_x)_y\). Continuous mixed second partials can be interchanged. Differentiate repeatedly before substituting a point.
If \(F(x,y,z)=0\) defines \(z\) locally and \(F_z\ne0\), then \(z_x=-F_x/F_z\) and \(z_y=-F_y/F_z\).
When computing \(F_x,F_y,F_z\), hold the other inputs constant. When differentiating the identity, remember that \(z\) depends on \(x,y\).
Existence of partial derivatives alone does not guarantee continuity or differentiability.

guides.title: Tangent planes and linear approximations
body: Linearization: \(L(x,y)=f(a,b)+f_x(a,b)(x-a)+f_y(a,b)(y-b)\). The tangent plane is \(z=L(x,y)\).
Differential: \(df=f_x\,dx+f_y\,dy\), with an additional \(f_z\,dz\) term for three inputs.
\(\Delta f\) is the exact new value minus the old value; \(df\) approximates it.
Estimated maximum error: \(|df|\le|f_x|\varepsilon_x+|f_y|\varepsilon_y\). Relative error is \(|df|/|f|\); multiply by \(100\) for a percentage.
Continuous first partials near the point guarantee differentiability. A zero partial means no first-order contribution, not necessarily zero actual change.

guides.title: Chain rule and related rates
body: Along a path, \(df/dt=f_xx'+f_yy'+f_zz'\).
For two parameters, \(f_s=f_xx_s+f_yy_s+f_zz_s\), and similarly for \(f_t\). Include every dependency path.
In \(G(u(s,t),v(s,t))\), evaluate the outer derivatives \(G_u,G_v\) at \((u,v)\), not at \((s,t)\).
For \(F(x,y)=0\), implicit differentiation gives \(y'=-F_x/F_y\) when \(F_y\ne0\).
Use signed rates and consistent units in related-rate problems. With explicit time dependence, \(dT/dt=T_xx'+T_yy'+T_t\).
Change per unit time and change per unit distance are different quantities.

guides.title: Directional derivatives and gradients
body: The gradient is the vector of partial derivatives. For a unit vector \(\mathbf u\), \(D_{\mathbf u}f=\nabla f\cdot\mathbf u\).
Toward \(Q\) from \(P\), normalize \(Q-P\) before taking the dot product.

Maximum rate: \(\|
abla f\|\), in direction \(
abla f/\|
abla f\|\). Minimum rate: \(-\|
abla f\|\), in the opposite direction. Perpendicular directions have zero rate.
For \(F=c\) with nonzero gradient, the tangent plane is \(\nabla F(P)\cdot(\mathbf r-P)=0\); the normal line is \(\mathbf r=P+t\nabla F(P)\).
Along a path, \(df/dt=\nabla f\cdot\mathbf r'\). A zero directional derivative at one point does not make a straight path a level curve.

guides.title: Local and absolute extrema
body: Critical points satisfy \(f_x=f_y=0\), or occur where a partial is undefined. A candidate need not be an extremum.
With continuous second partials, let \(D=f_{xx}f_{yy}-(f_{xy})^2\).
If \(D>0\) and \(f_{xx}>0\): local minimum. If \(D>0\) and \(f_{xx}<0\): local maximum. If \(D<0\): saddle. If \(D=0\): inconclusive.
A continuous function on a closed bounded region attains absolute extrema. Check interior candidates, every boundary segment, and endpoints; compare original function values.
When \(D=0\), use signs, factorization, sums of squares, or paths. State the extremal values and all attaining points.
A nonstrict minimum permits nearby points with equal values; a strict minimum does not.

guides.title: Lagrange multipliers
body:
For one constraint \(g=c\), solve \(
abla f=\lambda
abla g\) with the constraint. The usual condition is \(
abla g
e\mathbf0\); check exceptional points separately.
Do not divide by variables or multipliers before checking their zero cases. A finite candidate list does not guarantee absolute extrema on an unbounded set.
For a region \(g\le c\), check both the interior and the boundary.
Optimize squared distance first, then take its square root. Include all physical restrictions in applied problems.

With two constraints, solve \(
abla f=\lambda
abla g+\mu
abla h\) together with both constraints. The constraint gradients must be linearly independent.

guides.title: Top-down design and dictionaries
body: Start with the whole goal, divide it into coherent major tasks, and refine each task until its implementation is clear. Sibling tasks should have distinct responsibilities. Several reasonable decompositions may exist.

Root: no parent. Node: any element. Parent/child: adjacent levels. Leaf: no children. A leaf does not have to be on the deepest level. Hierarchies manage complexity but can hide connections across branches.

A dictionary maps keys to values. Keys are unique; values may repeat. d[key] looks up a key, not a position. Assigning an existing key replaces its value; assigning a new key adds a pair. Accessing a missing key raises KeyError.

key in d checks exact keys, not values or substrings. for key in d iterates over keys; use d[key] to read each corresponding value. len(d) counts pairs. Update existing values freely; avoid adding/deleting keys while directly iterating over the dictionary.
Initialize a missing key once; update on every occurrence. Do not reset a count each time you see the key.

Lecture 8 teaches {}, key indexing/assignment, membership, and direct iteration. This bank does not require get, items, values, pop, dictionary comprehensions, or other methods from a broader dictionary guide.
Source: Lecture8.pdf pp11-18,19-25,28-32

guides.title: Functions, scope, and shared objects
body: def records a function; its body runs when called. Parameters are the local names in the header; arguments are supplied at the call. return immediately exits the function. print displays text; it does not substitute for returning a result. Reaching the end without return gives None.
return a, b returns one tuple. x, y = f() unpacks by position. Tuple indexing and slicing work, but replacing a tuple slot raises TypeError. A mutable list stored inside a tuple can still change.

Each call gets local parameter/variable bindings. Reassigning a numeric or string parameter does not change the caller variable. A function can read a global if not shadowed; assigning to a name makes it local unless declared global. Reading such a local before assigning it raises UnboundLocalError.

a[0] = 9 changes a shared list; a = [9] only rebinds local a. For lists, a += [9] mutates while a = a + [9] rebinds. Dictionaries also share mutations through passed references. b = a aliases a list; b = a[:] makes a new outer list, not a recursive copy of nested lists.

Omitted trailing arguments use defaults; an explicit zero does not. In the taught positional headers, required parameters precede defaulted ones. Put a docstring first in the body describing purpose, inputs, outputs, and relevant units. Prefer arguments and returned results over hidden global dependencies.

Bind arguments -> run the body in order -> track shared-object mutations separately -> stop at return -> assign/use the returned object in the caller. Keep a separate row of local variables for every call.

body.code:
def split_total(total, people=2):
    """Return equal integer share and leftover units."""
    return total // people, total % people
share, leftover = split_total(17, 5)  # 3, 2
